items.readme: # NX2navi **Join the official NX2navi update discord server: https://discord.com/invite/uf6gSrsPpq** **NX2navi** is a static recompilation of *The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time* for Nintendo Switch 2 (game version 1.1.1) into a native x86-64 application for Windows, with a Vulkan renderer ([docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md)). > [!IMPORTANT] > **No game files are included.** You need your own legally obtained copy of the game, dumped from your own console. > Instructions for obtaining those files will not be provided. > > The game is built from your files on your machine, so the result contains the game. It is for your own use. Do not share it. ## Status Early development, playable. Kokiri Forest, Kakariko Village, Death Mountain Trail and its crater, the Temple of Time and the Great Fairy fountains play at 60 fps and above on current GPUs, from the title screen and from saves. Visual bugs and occasional crashes are still expected ([Known issues](#known-issues)). Report problems as issues, following [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Features - Native code, not emulation - 60 fps by default, or a limit of 30 to 240 fps, the display's refresh rate or unlimited - Native widescreen and ultrawide (the window's shape, 21:9 or 32:9) with the HUD, menus and movies kept 16:9 - Resolutions above the game's 1440p: 1800p, 4K, 5K or the window's own size, sharp on high-DPI displays - Upscaling and anti-aliasing: NVIDIA DLSS (DLAA, Quality, Balanced, Performance, Ultra Performance; RTX GPUs) or AMD FSR 3.1 (Native AA and the same modes; any GPU), which render the 3D scene at the mode's share and keep the HUD sharp; or AMD FSR 1 or bilinear scaling to the window, with a sharpness setting; black bars or stretch - Frame generation with AMD FSR 3.1 (any GPU): a generated frame between every two the game draws, with the HUD kept out of it, for about twice the frame rate on a fast display; in a window of another shape than the picture, frames are generated inside the picture only, so the black bars stay clean - HDR on HDR displays: the game's own native HDR, or an enhanced HDR made from its SDR picture - Every shader prepared when the game is built, and the pipelines met in play built again in the background at each start, so play does not stop to compile them; a draw that must wait for its pipeline has it built on worker threads, never on the game's drawing thread - In-game settings menu (F1, or Minus and Plus together on a gamepad) and performance overlay (F10) - Keyboard, mouse and gamepads with remapping, Nintendo or Xbox button layout, rumble and gyro; the game follows whichever connected gamepad you press - Stereo or 5.1 surround sound output - Docked or handheld console mode - The game's textures stay compressed (BC3, about half the video memory at the same speed) unless the PC has 20 GiB of video memory and 48 GiB of RAM, as Windows counts video memory against the system's commit limit ## Installing Download `NX2navi-Setup-.exe` from the releases and start it next to your `.nup` dump. It is the only file you need. The launcher it installs finds the dump, downloads the build tools, builds the game on your PC (10 to 25 minutes, once) and starts it; afterwards it keeps the port up to date and rebuilds only what changed ([docs/launcher.md](docs/launcher.md)). [docs/README-BuildKit.md](docs/README-BuildKit.md) describes the same build by hand, [docs/building.md](docs/building.md) building from source. Settings are in the in-game menu and in `nx2navi.ini` ([nx2navi.ini.example](nx2navi.ini.example) lists every key). Controls: [docs/controls.md](docs/controls.md). Requirements: Windows 10 or later; an x86-64 CPU with SSE4.2 (AVX2/FMA machines get a faster build); 16 GB of RAM; about 30 GB free for the game and 1.5 GB for the launcher and its tools; a GPU with Vulkan 1.3, `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` and `VK_EXT_mesh_shader`. The setup is not signed, so SmartScreen warns on its first start. ## Known issues - The first start after an install or update, and the first visit to an area, can pause briefly while the graphics driver builds what it has not seen; later starts are smooth. - A rare crash in the game's particle code. - DLSS Frame Generation is not offered yet: AMD FSR 3.1 frame generation works on every GPU, NVIDIA's included. ## License The source is public to read. Its additions and changes are all rights reserved ([LICENSE-ADDITIONS](LICENSE-ADDITIONS)): no part of them may be copied or published without written permission. The base import stays under its [MIT License](LICENSE), and third-party code keeps its own license ([THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md)). No license grants anything for Nintendo's game. NX2navi is an independent, non-commercial fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Nintendo. *The Legend of Zelda*, *Ocarina of Time* and *Nintendo Switch* are trademarks of Nintendo. ## Building from source [docs/building.md](docs/building.md) lists the toolchain and the steps. Everything the build writes stays under `build\` and `generated\`, which git ignores; run `tools/check_content.py` before a commit.

items.title: Sandflow-ai/sand3d
items.description: 3D modeling in Python, built for LLMs.
items.readme:
sand3d

**3D modeling in Python, built for LLMs.** sand3d is a Python library for writing 3D objects as short programs: profiles, solids, edits, frames, joints and assemblies, over Blender's `bpy`. A program says *how* a shape is made, part by part and in its own words, so a model writes it in a few hundred tokens and a person can read it.

 Website ·  Docs ·  Datasets ·  Explorer

## Why sand3d


How it is measured, part by part

- **Short.** A part takes 2 to 6× fewer tokens than the same part in Blender Python, CadQuery or FeatureScript ([details](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/tokens.html)). - **The whole API fits in a prompt**, about 3,600 tokens ([the API](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/api.html)). - **Named, not computed.** Parts, edges and faces are reached by name, never by hand-computed coordinates. - **Deterministic.** The same program builds the same mesh, bit for bit. ## A whole object, part by part

A front-loading washing machine in 38 lines of code ([play it and read it](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/gallery.html)): the cabinet, the drum, the door with its glass and handle, the detergent drawer and the dial, each a named part, and four joints that say how they move. ```python door = s3d.group("door", ring, glass, handle) # the handle and the glass move with it s3d.joint("door_hinge", door, hinge, axis="-Z", range=(0, 143)) s3d.joint("drum_spin", drum, front.move(0, 400), kind="continuous") s3d.joint("drawer_slide", drawer, top_band.move(150), kind="prismatic", axis="+X", range=(0, 200)) s3d.joint("dial_turn", dial, top_band.move(-150), kind="continuous") return s3d.assembly("washing_machine", cab, drum, door, drawer, dial, front=front) ``` ## Export: GLB, URDF, USD, OBJ, STL One call; the file's extension names the format; lengths in metres. ```python s3d.export(machine, "washer.glb") # or .urdf, .usda, .obj, .stl ``` | format | what it carries | for | |---|---|---| | **GLB** | meshes, materials, the joints in each node's extras, at the current pose | the web, viewers, game engines | | **URDF** | a link per moving part, its joints and their limits, at rest; OBJ meshes beside it | ROS, PyBullet, MuJoCo, Isaac | | **USDA** | the same tree in OpenUSD (UsdGeom, UsdPhysics), with the materials | Omniverse, Isaac Sim, USD pipelines | | **OBJ**, **STL** | the meshes alone, at the current pose: OBJ Y up, binary STL Z up | any 3D tool, slicers | `.usd`, `.usdc` and `.usdz` come from the `.usda` through USD's own tools (`usdcat`, `usdzip`). The scene is also an ordinary Blender scene, for anything else Blender writes. ## Install Python 3.13 (recommended) or 3.11. Blender comes with it, as the `bpy` module: 5.2 LTS on Python 3.13, 4.5 LTS on Python 3.11; CI runs bpy 5.2. ```bash pip install sand3d # or, in a uv project: uv add sand3d ``` `bpy` has no wheel for Python 3.12, nor for Intel Macs from 5.2 on: there, use Python 3.11. ## A first program ```python import sand3d as s3d def bracket(w=80, d=40, t=6, hole_d=6.6, pitch=50): plate = s3d.extrude("plate", s3d.rect(w, d, r=4), t) s3d.hole(plate, hole_d, on=s3d.grid(2, 1, pitch, 0)) s3d.fillet(plate, 1, edges="top") return plate s3d.export(bracket(), "bracket.glb") ``` Millimetres by default. Every verb with code that runs and its render: [the quickstart](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/quickstart.html); objects to play joint by joint: [the gallery](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/gallery.html); every signature: [the API](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/api.html). The programs themselves: [docs/examples/](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/tree/main/docs/examples/) and [programs/](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/tree/main/programs/). ## Give it to your LLM Put [docs/api.md](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/blob/main/docs/api.md) in the system prompt: the rules of the vocabulary, every signature, and worked examples, in about 3 600 tokens; [llms.txt](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/blob/main/llms.txt) points a model at it. For objects of several parts, [the guidelines](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/guidelines.html) give the eight rules of an assembly program: the plan first, then the details, then the parts. ## What is in it Everything on one flat `s3d.` surface: | family | verbs | |---|---| | profiles | `rect` `circle` `slot` `polygon` `poly` `arc` `spline` `superellipse` `text` `offset` `stroke` … (16) | | solids and paths | `extrude` `revolve` `sweep` `loft` `wire` `helix` `box` `cylinder` `tube` `sphere` `torus` `dome` … (15) | | edits | `cut` `join` `intersect` `split` `hole` `pocket` `fillet` `chamfer` `shell` `dent` … (15) | | frames and placement | `Frame` `face` `edge` `bbox` `local` `at` `transform` `grid` `ring` `along` `snap` | | articulation | `joint` `pose` `seat` | | assembly | `group` `assembly` `attach` `export` `units` `fingerprint` … (8) | | parts and materials | `gear` `knurl` `thread` `material` | No category verbs (`chair()`, `table()`): a category is a program written *in* sand3d. ## Datasets sand3d programs for five sources of 3D objects, on Hugging Face under CC BY 4.0.

sand3d-objaverse · Objaverse
Everyday objects from Objaverse, each rebuilt as a program.
sand3d-cad · CAD
Mechanical parts from public CAD models.
sand3d-articraft · Articraft
Articulated objects from Articraft, their joints declared.

sand3d-simready · SimReady
Simulation-ready assets from NVIDIA SimReady.
sand3d-automate · AutoMate
Mechanical assemblies from AutoMate, each part a function of its program.
Browse them in [the explorer](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Sandflow/sand3d-explorer), or all five in [the collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/Sandflow/sand3d-6aec268fbdcd3bc174236168). ## Citation If you use sand3d in your work, please cite it. `CITATION.cff` holds the same, and GitHub shows it as "Cite this repository". ```bibtex @misc{sand3d2026, author = {Neveu, Thibault and Loy, Andr{\'e}a}, title = {sand3d}, year = {2026}, note = {Version 1.6.3}, url = {https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d} } ``` ## Contributing and license How the library is built, tested and versioned: [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). Apache License 2.0: see [LICENSE](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/blob/main/LICENSE).

items.title: livliv-dev/player
items.description: A lightweight 2.5D character player for the web, with lip sync and webcam face tracking.
items.readme:
A lightweight 2.5D character player for the web, with lip sync and webcam face tracking. A few lines of code put a character in a page, a stream overlay or an app.
Comes with 21 featured characters in different styles, ready to use.

English · 中文 · 日本語 · Tiếng Việt

- WebGL2, no dependencies, about 30 KB gzipped for the core - Lip sync (microphone, audio, video) and webcam face tracking (MediaPipe), both in the browser, imported only when you need them - Plays LivLiv, VRM and PNGTuber characters through the same API - 21 featured characters in [`characters/`](characters/), ready to use ## Try it - **Online**: the examples run on [livliv-dev.github.io/player](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/). - **Here**: `npm install && npm run build`, serve this folder with any static server and open `/example/demo.html` (expressions, actions, microphone, camera; `?model=../characters//` picks another character). `/example/png.html` and `/example/vrm.html` show a PNGTuber and a VRM. - **On livliv.ai**: each character's page there plays it with the same renderer. Start at [livliv.ai/discover](https://livliv.ai/discover). ## Project LivLiv We want the art of creating characters to belong to everyone. We're open-sourcing our AI tools for character creation, the player and its playback protocol, and a stage where your characters can meet an audience. Come say hello on [Discord](https://discord.gg/ac5qF36T2H) and follow us on [X (Twitter)](https://x.com/livliv_ai). ## Use it in your page ```sh npm install @livliv-dev/player ``` ```js import { Player } from '@livliv-dev/player' const player = new Player(document.querySelector('canvas')) await player.load('characters/k01/') // a folder with model.json and textures/, or a .livliv file player.setExpression('smile') // ids are in player.expressions player.act('nod') player.params.mouthOpen = 0.6 // 0..1 ``` Lip sync and face tracking: ```js import { createSpeech } from '@livliv-dev/player/voice' import { startFaceTracking } from '@livliv-dev/player/tracking' // needs @mediapipe/tasks-vision const speech = createSpeech(player) button.onclick = () => { speech.unlock(); speech.say('/reply.mp3') } await startFaceTracking(player) ``` A VRM or a PNGTuber, on the same API: ```js import { BodyPlayer } from '@livliv-dev/player/body' import { VrmBody } from '@livliv-dev/player/vrm' // needs three and @pixiv/three-vrm import { PngBody } from '@livliv-dev/player/png' const vrm = new BodyPlayer(canvasA, new VrmBody()) await vrm.load('/avatars/me.vrm') const png = new BodyPlayer(canvasB, new PngBody()) await png.load({ closed: 'me-closed.png', open: 'me-open.png' }) ``` The whole API is in [API.md](API.md): options, params, expressions and actions, drivers, VRM and PNGTuber characters, the limits on untrusted files, the model package and the format version. The LivLiv package format (`.livliv`, `model.json` v4) is in [FORMAT.md](FORMAT.md), with a JSON Schema in [`schema/`](schema/); packages exported before v4 are described in [FORMAT-v3.md](FORMAT-v3.md) and still play. > The npm package is the player alone. The featured characters are in this repository's [`characters/`](characters/): copy > the ones you use next to your page, with their licence. ## Featured characters `characters/` holds 21 characters, ready to `load()`. They carry a small LivLiv mark in the bottom-right corner, which the player draws. They are **not** covered by the Apache License. Most were made by LivLiv: use those free for personal, non-commercial projects with credit ("Characters: LivLiv (livliv.ai)"); don't sell them, use them commercially or train AI models on them. Nana is LivLiv's mascot. The terms are in [characters/LICENSE.md](characters/LICENSE.md). Kujira, Kujira Q and Pen come from other people's work: that licence and that credit don't cover them. Their sources, credits and terms are in [characters/CREDITS.md](characters/CREDITS.md). Each also has a `cover.webp` (512 x 768, about 50 KB), its first frame without the mark. `player.load(source, { poster })` shows it on the canvas until the first frame. To have it before any script has run, put it under the canvas with `object-fit: contain` and fade the character in over it, as [example/loading.js](example/loading.js) does. | id | name | id | name | id | name | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | `k01` | Sena | `d01` | Yui | `v01` | Aster | | `k02` | Elio | `d02` | Leo | `v03` | Mira | | `char06` | Aoi | `d03` | Nana | `v04` | Kai | | `char07` | Sora | `d03ft` | Nana (refined) | `v05` | Lilith | | `s01` | Hana | `p01` | Kujira | `v06` | Usa | | `q02` | Mochi | `p02` | Kujira Q | `v07` | Stella | | `q03` | Kotaro | `p03` | Pen | `w01` | Max | ## Characters of your own You can bring in a PNGTuber's pictures, or a VRM (drawn with three.js); or make a character of your own from one picture on [livliv.ai](https://livliv.ai). - **A PNGTuber**: two pictures (mouth closed, mouth open), and two more with the eyes closed if you have them. - **A VRM**: from VRoid Studio or any tool that exports VRM 0.x or 1.0. - **A LivLiv model**: make one from a picture on [livliv.ai](https://livliv.ai), then download its model package from the character's page (**Model package**): a `.livliv` file. Pass it to `load()` as it is (a URL, or the `File` someone picked), or unzipped as a folder. Packages on the free plan carry the LivLiv mark, and the player draws it. ## About the player and the characters LivLiv Player and the `.livliv` format are LivLiv's own work. They use no Live2D software or Cubism SDK and do not read `.moc3` or `.cmo3` files. "Live2D" is a trademark of Live2D Inc.; LivLiv is not affiliated with it. Making a character on livliv.ai uses AI. The player itself only plays: it calls no AI service and reads only the files you point it at. Face tracking runs Google's MediaPipe in the browser, and camera images stay on the device; API.md has the networking details. The featured characters in this repository were made on LivLiv too, also with AI; Kujira, Kujira Q and Pen adapt other people's characters ([credits](characters/CREDITS.md)). Refined Nana (`d03ft`) also has swinging parts and head-turn keyforms added with LivLiv's own tools. A package's `meta.author` and `meta.license` record who made it and on what terms: keep them and follow them. When you show a character made with LivLiv in public, say that AI was used to make it, and don't present it as hand-drawn or hand-rigged. ## Embed without code ```html ``` The same `/live/` page has a transparent background and works as an OBS Browser Source.\ (Powered by [https://livliv.ai](https://livliv.ai)) ## Develop ```sh git clone https://github.com/livliv-dev/player cd player npm install npm run check # types npm run build # dist/: index.js, tracking.js, voice.js, body.js, png.js, vrm.js (ES modules), chunks/ and types/ npm test # unit and fuzz tests (Node 22.18 or newer, no browser) npm run test:browser # every featured character drawn in headless Chromium; once: npx playwright-core install chromium-headless-shell npm run test:engines # a sample on Firefox and WebKit, where WebGL2 starts (a GPU or a software GL); once: npx playwright-core install firefox webkit ``` `src/runtime/` is the renderer and motion code livliv.ai runs; this repository is published from it. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Security reports: [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Browser support WebGL2 and ES2023: Chrome / Edge 97+, Firefox 104+, Safari 15.4+. Tested on current desktop browsers, not yet on phones. ## License The code is under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE) (see also [NOTICE](NOTICE)). The featured characters have their own licence, [characters/LICENSE.md](characters/LICENSE.md). Neither licence covers the LivLiv name and logos. ## Thanks Thanks to 上善无形, ZipZipPipe and 贱兔死顺盖, whose characters Kujira, Kujira Q and Pen are based on: see [characters/CREDITS.md](characters/CREDITS.md).

items.title: CzJam/gjgjxweb
items.readme:
# 搞机工具箱 Web - 网页版 Android 玩机工具 ##

使用教程  在线体验

《搞机工具箱》是一款ADB图形化工具。 本项目移植于个人开发的 [《搞机工具箱》PC版](https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1QvHhzLELb) 。借助 [Tango](https://github.com/yume-chan/ya-webadb) 实现了 WebADB，并通过 [xterm.js](https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js) 打通 Android 原生 Shell 交互式终端，可运行在基于Chromium内核的浏览器中，实现免下载、免安装的跨平台使用体验。 [作者 @晨钟酱Official](https://space.bilibili.com/251013709) [官网: jamcz.com](https://jamcz.com) ## 功能 | 页面 | 主要功能 | | --- | --- | | 主页 | 设备与系统信息、CPU 频率、主板 ID 隐藏、重启、关机、重启至 Bootloader / Fastbootd / Recovery / EDL | | 软件管理 | 包名与前台活动读取、启用/禁用、运行、强行停止、卸载与保留数据卸载、清除数据、软件信息、恢复系统软件、卸载锁定、操作记录、Google 套件批量管理 | | 安装与文件传输 | APK 安装、拆分 APK 安装、推送文件、提取安装包 | | 显示控制 | 分辨率、显示密度（DPI / dp）、按键模拟、截图 | | 系统界面 | 状态栏图标隐藏、时钟与快捷设置、沉浸模式、Wi-Fi 网络检测相关设置 | | 电池管理 | 电池信息、电池参数模拟与恢复、定时统计、可选功率记录、CSV 导出 | | 无极调节 | 字体大小倍数、窗口/过渡/程序动画倍率、自动锁屏时间 | | 控机脚本 | 脚本编辑与导入导出、命令插入、文件关联、部分 BAT 语法解释执行 | | ADB 终端 | Android Shell 交互会话、ANSI 显示、命令历史、补全、复制、清屏与中断 | | 软件设置 | 默认启动页、主题配色、界面缩放、CPU 更新间隔、文件接收路径、安装与截图选项、设置导入导出 | 当前界面提供 **USB 有线连接**。功能是否生效取决于设备的 Android 版本、ROM 和 ADB Shell 权限。进入 Fastboot 的按钮仅发送重启命令，本工具暂不提供 Fastboot 刷机功能。 ## 快速开始 ### 使用条件 - 使用支持 WebUSB 的 Chrome 或 Edge 或 其他基于Chromium内核的浏览器（不分操作系统，手机安装Chrome也能用）。 - 手机开启开发者选项和 USB 调试，使用 USB 数据线连接电脑。 - 通过本机 `localhost` / `127.0.0.1` 或 HTTPS 网站访问页面。 - Windows 需要能够正常识别手机的 ADB USB 接口，且手机端同意授权请求。 ### 本地运行 仓库默认为 **HTML、CSS、JavaScript的前端分离版** ，同时提供AIO的 **单HTML整合版**。页面和第三方依赖均保存在本地，可直接本地部署或执行，无需构建或安装 npm 依赖。 #### 方法1: 整合版 下载项目docs中的index.html。已内嵌完整依赖，使用Chromium内核浏览器直接本地运行。 #### 方法2: 分离版 1. 下载并解压完整项目，保留目录结构。 2. 安装 [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/)，在包含 `server.cjs` 的目录打开终端。 3. 运行： ```powershell node server.cjs ``` 4. 使用 Chrome 或 Edge 打开 [http://127.0.0.1:8124](http://127.0.0.1:8124)。 5. 点击“连接设备”，在浏览器中选择手机；首次连接时，在手机上确认 USB 调试授权。 按 `Ctrl+C` 停止服务。服务只监听本机地址 `127.0.0.1`。 若默认端口被占用，可在 PowerShell 中更换端口： ```powershell $env:PORT = "8080" node server.cjs ``` 随后打开 [http://127.0.0.1:8080](http://127.0.0.1:8080)。也可以使用其他能够正确提供 ES 模块的静态网页服务器。 **请通过网页服务器打开分离版。** 直接双击 `index.html` 会使用 `file://` 地址，外部 ES 模块可能因浏览器的跨源限制而加载失败，导致连接按钮不可用。参见 [MDN：JavaScript 模块](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Modules)。 ## 部署到网站 将本目录中的完整文件上传到支持 HTTPS 的静态托管服务或 Web 服务器，以 `index.html` 为入口即可。第三方依赖已包含在 `js/vendor/` 中，运行时无需额外从 CDN 下载依赖，也不需要部署 ADB 后端。 - 保留 `index.html`、`css/`、`js/`、`assets/` 的相对路径。 - 对外提供服务时使用 HTTPS。本机回环地址属于浏览器认可的可信来源，因此本地开发可以使用 HTTP。参见 [MDN：安全上下文](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Secure_Contexts)。 - JavaScript 应返回有效的 JavaScript MIME 类型，例如 `text/javascript`；CSS 应返回 `text/css`。不要将它们统一返回为 `application/octet-stream`。 - 如果自行改为 CDN 引用，脚本、样式和模块依赖也应使用 HTTPS，避免被浏览器作为混合内容屏蔽。 - `server.cjs` 是可选的本地启动工具；部署到静态托管平台后，访问者无需安装 Node.js。 WebUSB 的授权和使用条件可参考 [Chrome WebUSB 文档](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/capabilities/usb)。 ## 目录结构 ```text . ├── index.html # 页面结构与模块入口 ├── README.md # 项目说明 ├── LICENSE # 项目 GPLv3 许可证全文 ├── server.cjs # 本地静态服务器（Node.js 标准库） ├── LICENSE-Tango.txt # Tango 相关组件许可 ├── LICENSE-xterm.txt # xterm.js 相关组件许可 ├── assets/ │ └── favicon.svg # 页面图标 ├── docs/ │ └── index.html # 完整本地运行文件 ├── css/ │ ├── styles.css # 工具箱样式 │ └── xterm.css # 终端样式 └── js/ ├── app.js # 页面初始化、交互、连接状态与设置 ├── core.js # 命令执行与各功能逻辑 ├── transport.js # Tango / WebUSB 连接与传输 ├── terminal.js # 交互式终端会话 ├── batch.js # BAT 语法子集解释器 └── vendor/ # 本地第三方依赖 ``` ## 终端与脚本 ### ADB 终端 终端连接的是手机上的 Android Shell，可直接输入 Shell 命令： ```sh getprop ro.product.model wm size settings get system font_scale ``` 同一连接中的终端会话保留当前目录和环境变量；切换页面不会重新创建会话。历史记录和补全由设备上的 Shell 提供，`Ctrl+C` 可中断正在运行的命令。断开设备或重新启动终端会结束当前会话。 ### BAT 脚本 控机脚本通过 JavaScript 解释部分 BAT 语法，将其中的 ADB 操作转换为浏览器端调用，**不会启动 Windows 的 `cmd.exe` 或执行电脑上的 EXE**。 例如，可以导入并执行以下脚本： ```bat @echo off echo 读取设备型号 adb shell getprop ro.product.model timeout /t 1 adb shell wm size ``` 支持的语法包括 `echo`、`rem`、`set`、`set /a`、`set /p`、变量替换、标签与 `goto`、部分 `if` 条件、`if errorlevel`、多行括号形式的 `for /l`、`timeout`、`choice /t`、`pause` 和 `exit /b`。具体支持范围以解释器实现为准。 涉及 `adb push`、`adb install` 等本地文件操作时，需要先在页面中关联对应文件。浏览器无法仅凭脚本中的 Windows 路径读取电脑文件。 这套解释器兼容的是 BAT 语法子集。依赖外部程序、PowerShell、`for /f` 或复杂 CMD 语法的脚本需要调整；遇到不支持的命令时会报告错误。 ## 数据保存与文件下载 - **设置、脚本文本、软件操作记录**：保存在当前网站的浏览器本地存储中。清理网站数据会删除这些内容；设置和脚本可通过页面提供的功能导出备份。 - **ADB 身份密钥**：由 Tango 保存在浏览器 IndexedDB 中。可在断开设备后，通过软件设置清除。 - **网站地址变更**：不同协议、域名或端口使用独立的网站存储，迁移部署地址后可能需要重新授权和导入设置。 - **截图与电池统计**：需要及时下载保存，当前页面内的临时数据不会跨刷新保留。 - **电池 CSV**：文件名使用连接设备读取到的机型名称和日期时间，例如 `一加 15T_2026-11-03_14-30-00.csv`；无法读取营销名称时回退到系统型号。 - **下载目录**：可在支持的浏览器中授权保存目录；未授权时使用普通浏览器下载。截图“下载后删除手机原图”仅在确认写入所选目录后执行，普通浏览器下载会保留手机原图。 设备命令通过浏览器与手机之间的 USB 连接执行，不经过本项目的远程 ADB 服务。文件与目录访问需要用户通过浏览器选择或授权。 ## 常见问题 | 问题 | 排查方法 | | --- | --- | | 连接按钮是灰色的 | 使用 Chrome / Edge，通过本地服务器或 HTTPS 打开完整目录；检查开发者工具中的模块加载错误、404 和 MIME 类型错误。 | | 提示当前 ADB 接口被占用 | 在任务管理器中结束占用接口的 `adb.exe`，关闭其他 ADB 工具及已连接设备的 WebADB 页面，再重新连接。 | | 浏览器找不到设备 | 检查 USB 调试、数据线与 USB 接口，以及 Windows 下的 ADB 驱动；确认数据线支持数据传输。 | | 手机没有授权弹框 | 解锁手机并检查 USB 调试；已有有效授权时可能不会再次弹框。仍无法连接时，可在手机开发者选项撤销 USB 调试授权后重试。 | | 资源被屏蔽为 `mixed-content` | HTTPS 页面引用了 HTTP 资源，需将相关资源及其依赖改为 HTTPS。 | | 提示 `application/octet-stream` 或 MIME 错误 | 检查静态资源服务器的响应头，按扩展名设置正确的 JavaScript / CSS 类型。 | | 命令返回权限不足、设置不生效 | Android 版本、厂商 ROM 和系统策略可能限制 ADB Shell 权限；部分设备还需开启厂商提供的 USB 调试安全选项。 | | CPU 频率、功率或主板 ID 无法读取 | 部分设备不开放对应系统节点。功率记录依赖设备提供的电流、电压等数据，不等同于外接充电功率计测量值。 | | 关闭或刷新页面后连接断开 | USB 会话依附于当前页面，需要重新连接；请提前下载需要保留的数据。 | ## 开发与反馈 本分离版直接使用原生 JavaScript ES 模块。修改后启动 `server.cjs` 并刷新页面即可查看效果，无需执行依赖安装或打包命令。 - 修改页面布局：`index.html`。 - 修改样式：`css/styles.css`。 - 修改页面交互与设置：`js/app.js`。 - 修改设备命令和功能逻辑：`js/core.js`。 - 修改 USB 连接、终端或脚本解释：分别查看 `js/transport.js`、`js/terminal.js`、`js/batch.js`。 - 更新第三方组件时，检查模块引用与接口兼容性，并保留相应的版权及许可证文件。 欢迎通过仓库的 Issues 反馈问题或提交 Pull Request。反馈时请提供工具版本、浏览器版本、电脑系统、设备型号、Android / ROM 版本、复现步骤和相关错误信息。提交截图或命令输出前，请隐藏设备序列号、主板 ID 等个人设备信息。 涉及设备行为的修改，请说明实际测试设备及结果；未经实机验证的行为请明确注明。 ## 第三方项目 感谢以下开源项目： | 项目 | 使用组件与版本 | 许可 | | --- | --- | --- | | [Tango / ya-webadb](https://github.com/yume-chan/ya-webadb) | `@yume-chan/adb` 2.6.4、`adb-daemon-webusb` 2.3.2、`adb-credential-web` 2.1.0、`stream-extra` 2.6.1、`struct` 2.3.2、`event` 2.0.0、`async` 4.1.3、`no-data-view` 2.0.0 | [MIT](LICENSE-Tango.txt) | | [xterm.js](https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js) | `@xterm/xterm` 5.5.0、`@xterm/addon-fit` 0.10.0 | [MIT](LICENSE-xterm.txt) | ### 项目许可 本项目的原创代码采用 **GNU General Public License v3.0（GPL-3.0-only）**，许可证全文见 [LICENSE](LICENSE)。 Copyright (C) 2026 晨钟酱Official。 第三方组件保留各自的版权与 MIT 许可，详见 [LICENSE-Tango.txt](LICENSE-Tango.txt) 和 [LICENSE-xterm.txt](LICENSE-xterm.txt)。分发时请保留这些声明。 本软件按许可证所述提供，不附带任何担保。 ## 使用说明 本工具为全安卓通用软件。使用本工具则代表您有一定玩机知识储备。若盲目操作导致无法开机或丢失数据则后果自负，作者不承担任何责任。

items.title: mmdoctor/google-pro-helper
items.readme:
# Google Pro Helper

本仓库收录两个独立版本：浏览器扩展版与批量版，分别保留各自的目录结构和原有代码。

| 版本 | 目录 | 简介 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 浏览器扩展版 | [extension](./extension/) | 在浏览器中使用的扩展项目，包含扩展清单、弹窗页面、脚本与图标。 |
| 批量版 | [batch](./batch/) | 用于批量账号任务管理的本地控制台项目，包含网页界面、后端、启动脚本与测试。 |

## 目录结构

```text
google-pro-helper/
├── extension/   # 浏览器扩展版
├── batch/       # 批量版
├── .gitignore
└── README.md
```

## 浏览器扩展版


Linuxdo原帖在此:

[https://linux.do/t/topic/3123997](https://linux.do/t/topic/3123997)


（💰 免费激活 Google AI Pro 12 / 24 个月」| offer token 注入）


（我本人大部分号是用的是注册机批量搞的，原理都一样，总共整了七个目前都活过了半个月，不过被这么大批量薅，估计也活不久了）

> **在此提示，不要用大号！！！！**

### **1.在chrome浏览器上点击"加载未打包的拓展程序"，注意打开开发者模式**

![image](https://i0.hdslb.com/bfs/new_dyn/f6ecc1314583543aedb82bf0d950213e3747579686817540.png@1192w.webp)

### **2.然后打开 one.google.com/plans，按照拓展里步骤，先开12月的，注意正上方的绿色提示，和右下角的提示**

![image](https://i0.hdslb.com/bfs/new_dyn/5de4698ae0cd2a371a1ecb3e6727a8823747579686817540.png@1130w_1760h.webp)

![image](https://i0.hdslb.com/bfs/new_dyn/33147e398928380c614b5ae85bd50a903747579686817540.png@1192w.webp)

![image](https://i0.hdslb.com/bfs/new_dyn/2544ad49e1db82fb90999fe3355e6fbd3747579686817540.png@92h.webp)

### **3.然后选择pro套餐，进行绑卡（需要卡里有至少1u验证，u卡基本都行，测试卡：starryblu/maya/bybit/mexc/招行master/中行2233master/bitEU/wise/savo卡全都可以）付款前一定要看清，第一个步骤首月必定是0元的**

> PS：这里需要说明如果是已经给了折扣的情况，如下图，付款时有极大概率需要付款首月的youtube会员，小心别被反薅，正常显示的都是在下个月才收费

![image](https://i0.hdslb.com/bfs/new_dyn/b24d7dc8773238dce8883de6ac8fb5a13747579686817540.png@1192w.webp)

![image](https://i0.hdslb.com/bfs/new_dyn/9b5d510ce927dc364d468eb82cc7182e3747579686817540.png@1046w_1590h.webp)

### **4.然后如果不再出订购页面的话，不要着急，也不要取消订阅（其实取消了也无所谓）。**

先把拓展切换到六个月，再重新进入页面，接着点击切换到年付

就会再次出现订购页面，这里会出现2028.5.5付款（示例日期），不要担心，这个其实还是免费的，到2028.5.5才会付款；同样的方法再次操作，切换下一个6个月，就能实现2年pro会员了

![image](https://i0.hdslb.com/bfs/new_dyn/59a750f80e575523398a3cee77f0ae343747579686817540.png@1192w.webp)

> ps：
>
> 最后一定注意取消订阅，不要被反薅，因为附带有一个每月的youtube会员需要付费，不取消的话下个月就会被反薅

![image](https://i0.hdslb.com/bfs/new_dyn/c65340f450d8c110abd88de7f0faa99c3747579686817540.png@1192w.webp)

**L站佬友补充：**

> Fy6666:
>
> YouTube Premium Individual Add On无法使用。您可以单独订阅此套装中的其他商品。提示这样子怎么办呢？查了，是YouTube那个会员资格只有美国、加拿大、巴西、法国、德国、日本哦，这6个国家可以

> aikavvak12una:
>
> 账号地区不对可以直接先添加美国的付款方式就再订阅就行了
>
> 我的一个小号条款地区甚至是中国 🤣

更改play商店支付方式即可，和谷歌账号属地无关


## 批量版

**Google AI Pro (5 TB) 零成本两年 (US$0.00 -> 24个月) 全自动控制台**

> 以上述“零成本两年”为项目目标，不代表已验证的订阅结果。原说明中的“全程 0 扣费”不能作为保证，实际费用和权益以结账页面及上游结果为准。

### 一、运行环境要求
1. Windows 10 / 11 系统
2. 已安装 Google Chrome 浏览器（默认路径即可）
3. 已安装 Python 3.10 或更高版本（安装时勾选 Add Python to PATH）
4. 网络环境：本机开启美区（US）代理，或在控制台左侧填写代理模板

### 二、快速启动步骤
1. 首次使用请双击运行：【1_首次运行_安装依赖并启动.bat】
2. 之后日常使用直接双击：【2_启动控制台.bat】
3. 浏览器会自动打开控制台页面：http://127.0.0.1:8765

### 三、自定义填写支付卡 & 跑号说明
#### 1. 填写支付卡（必填）：
   - 在网页左侧【全局配置与内联免税绑卡】区域，填入你自己的 Visa 或 Mastercard 外币卡：
     * 卡号（16位数字）
     * 有效期（月 / 年，如 08 / 29）
     * 安全码（3位 CVC）
     * 持卡人英文姓名
     * 免税邮编默认已填好 97201（美国俄勒冈免税州），无需修改
   - 填写后点击【💾 保存配置】。
   - 注：脚本内置严格 0 元消费保护，仅在结账弹窗确认为 US$0.00 时才会点击订阅，全程 0 扣费。

#### 2. 批量导入 Google 账号：
   - 在网页右侧【批量放号导入区】粘贴账号（每行一个），支持以下任意格式：
     * 邮箱----密码----辅助邮箱
     * 邮箱----密码----辅助邮箱----2FA密钥
     * 邮箱----密码----2FA密钥
   - 点击【➕ 一键导入账号列表】。

#### 3. 开始全自动执行：
   - 点击单个账号右侧的【▶ 执行】或顶部的【▶ 批量全自动执行】。
   - 脚本会自动完成：
     - Step 1: 自动登录 Google 并通过辅助邮箱 / 2FA 验证
     - Step 2: 内联免税绑卡 + 首层 12 个月免费包 (US$0.00)
     - Step 3: 叠加二层 6 个月免费包 (US$0.00 -> 18个月)
     - Step 4: 叠加三层 6 个月免费包 (US$0.00 -> 24个月封顶)
     - Step 5: 自动前往 Google Play 取消自动续订，锁死 2 年到期权益并截图验真

### 四、隔离与敏感数据

- 浏览器扩展版位于 `extension/`，批量版位于 `batch/`，两者分目录存放。批量版原启动脚本使用当前 Python 环境安装依赖，未提供独立虚拟环境，不能宣称依赖完全隔离。
- 批量版按账号使用独立浏览器配置目录，但这不等于虚拟机或安全沙箱。
- 账号密码、2FA 密钥、支付卡信息和浏览器登录数据属于敏感信息；本地配置、浏览器配置目录、截图、日志及缓存不应提交到仓库。


## 使用入口

- **浏览器扩展版**：打开 Chrome 扩展管理页，开启开发者模式，选择“加载已解压的扩展程序”，加载 `extension` 目录。
- **批量版**：在 Windows 下进入 `batch` 目录，首次使用运行 `1_首次运行_安装依赖并启动.bat`，之后运行 `2_启动控制台.bat`。

两个版本独立使用。本次整理仅增加仓库分层和本页介绍，不修改项目源代码。

本地账号与支付配置（`config*.json`）、环境变量文件、缓存和运行数据不提交到仓库；批量版的配置请在本地填写。

items.title: shanselman/gputaskman
items.description: A GPU task manager for Windows, Linux, and WSL: per-process VRAM, GPU activity, and LLM model/KV-cache insights (Windows AMD and NVIDIA).
items.readme:
# gputaskman

**An `htop` for what's inside your GPU, not just how full it is.**

Windows + NVIDIA/AMD, with Linux and WSL support (NVIDIA everywhere, AMD and Intel on native Linux; see
[Linux and WSL](#linux-and-wsl)) and macOS on Apple Silicon (see [macOS](#macos-apple-silicon)). A terminal UI
that connects per-process GPU memory and engine activity with loaded runtimes, model files, and
LLM buffer breakdowns.

Task Manager says "15 GB used." This tries to answer: *by what? Model weights? KV cache?
Your browser? The desktop compositor? And why is so much GPU memory in system RAM?*

**Scope: local GPU workloads, not cloud services.** Decision models, vision, speech, LLM inference,
training/fine-tuning (including Unsloth), graphics, and video all belong here. Visibility varies:
process memory and engine activity are measured; identifying individual models and their work
requires supporting evidence. A PyTorch/CUDA DLL alone cannot identify a model or prove training,
and a mapped file does not prove that model is resident on the GPU or being exercised.
CPU-only, NPU-only, and cloud workloads are out of scope.

![Live GPU overview with an LLM's weights, KV cache, and compute buffer breakdown](docs/screenshots/overview.png)

> Early, experimental software. Device and process counters are measurements; classifications
> and GGUF-derived breakdowns are estimates. This does not dump VRAM or enumerate a game's textures.

## Install from PyPI

[gputaskman is on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/gputaskman/). No repository clone is needed:

```powershell
uv tool install gputaskman
gputaskman
```

Or, with [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io/):

```powershell
pipx install gputaskman
gputaskman
```

Works on Windows, Linux/WSL, and macOS with Python 3.11+ and the supported GPU/driver
configuration described below. Both installers keep the app in an isolated environment.
The shorter `gtm` command is also available. Upgrade with `uv tool upgrade gputaskman`
or `pipx upgrade gputaskman`. For Windows without Python, use the portable download below.

## Portable Windows download

The [Releases page](https://github.com/shanselman/gputaskman/releases) is where tagged builds
publish two portable ZIPs: `gputaskman-VERSION-windows-x64.zip` for Intel/AMD Windows PCs, and
`gputaskman-VERSION-windows-arm64.zip` for native Windows ARM64. These are separate native builds,
not a universal executable.

Extract the **entire ZIP**, keeping `_internal` beside `gputaskman.exe`. Open Windows Terminal
or PowerShell in the extracted folder:

```powershell
.\gputaskman.exe
.\gputaskman.exe --once
.\gputaskman.exe --json
```

No Python, uv, CUDA Toolkit, model download, or installation is needed. A supported GPU with a
current Windows WDDM driver is required. Builds are currently **unsigned**; code signing
and an installer are not part of this initial distribution. Each ZIP includes licenses and a
`.zip.sha256` companion file is published for integrity checks.

## Clone and run

Use **64-bit Windows 10/11**, an **NVIDIA or AMD GPU with a current WDDM driver**, and a terminal
(Windows Terminal is recommended). Live workload checks have included an RTX 4080 SUPER and an
RTX Spark N1X on Windows ARM64. CUDA workloads are supported on ARM64 with a compatible NVIDIA
driver and ARM64 CUDA runtime.

AMD live check: Radeon 860M Graphics on Windows 11 Enterprise build 26300, AMD driver 32.0.22050.1003.
During desktop/browser activity, WDDM reported per-process VRAM and AMD ADL reported GPU utilization,
clocks, and ASIC power; temperature, memory activity, and PCIe readings were unavailable. Vulkan/ROCm
workloads were not tested on this machine.

Install [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win) and
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) if needed. With WinGet:

```powershell
winget install --id Git.Git --exact
winget install --id astral-sh.uv --exact
```

Open a new PowerShell window so those tools are on `PATH`, then:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/shanselman/gputaskman.git
cd gputaskman
uv run --locked gputaskman
```

**That's it.** uv obtains the pinned Python version if needed, creates `.venv`, and installs
the locked dependencies. The first run needs internet access. There is no CUDA Toolkit,
Visual Studio, administrator session, API key, or model download required to monitor the GPU.
NVML ships with the NVIDIA driver; AMD ADL is supplied by supported AMD Windows drivers.

Already have Python 3.11+ and prefer pip?

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/shanselman/gputaskman.git
cd gputaskman
py -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install .
.\.venv\Scripts\gputaskman.exe
```

No PowerShell activation script or execution-policy change is needed. The pip route resolves
compatible dependencies; the uv route uses the checked-in lockfile.

If an alternate package index makes `--locked` report a stale lockfile on an unchanged checkout,
`uv run --frozen gputaskman` uses the checked-in lockfile without re-resolving it. `--frozen`
skips the consistency check, so do not use it after changing dependencies.

## Linux and WSL

Tagged releases include portable Linux builds: `gputaskman-VERSION-linux-x64.tar.gz` and
`gputaskman-VERSION-linux-arm64.tar.gz`. They need glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12,
or newer) and an NVIDIA driver (or, on native Linux, an AMD GPU on the `amdgpu` driver or an Intel GPU on `i915`), and work
natively, in containers, and in WSL:

```bash
tar -xzf gputaskman-VERSION-linux-x64.tar.gz
cd gputaskman-VERSION-linux-x64
./gputaskman
```

Or clone and run from source, in a Linux or WSL shell:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/shanselman/gputaskman.git
cd gputaskman
uv run --locked gputaskman
```

What can be measured depends on where it runs, and the UI says which mode it is in.

| | Native Linux | WSL, interop on (default) | WSL, interop off or `--no-host` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Device totals, load, temperature, power, clocks | NVML | NVML | NVML |
| Per-process VRAM | NVML, measured (in a container: owner matched, `*` or `?`) | Matched from the Windows host, marked `*` or `?` | `n/a` |
| Per-process GPU load | NVML (SM, encoder, decoder) | `n/a` for Linux processes | `n/a` |
| Spill / Paged | Not available (blank) | Windows rows only | Not available |
| WSL VM total, Windows apps | — | Windows host counters | — |
| Runtimes, model files, LLM breakdown | `/proc/<pid>/maps`, command line | Same | Same |

**Native Linux** reads per-process memory from NVML's running compute and graphics process lists
and per-process SM, encoder, and decoder load from NVML utilization samples. Linux has no
equivalent of WDDM's shared-memory or commit counters, so Spill and Paged stay blank rather than
showing zero. Only processes you can inspect are listed; other users' processes need `sudo`.

JSON uses `null` for unavailable counters, not a measured zero: spill/commit/paged values on
native Linux, and per-process engine load for WSL Linux rows. Native NVML engine readings remain
available even if NVML hides that process's VRAM. Windows host rows retain their measured counters.

**Containers** (Docker, Kubernetes, rented GPU boxes) need one more step: NVML reports *host*
PIDs, which mean nothing in the container's `/proc`, and the container cannot see the host PID of
its own processes. gputaskman pairs NVML's unresolved PIDs with the container's processes that
have `libcuda.so` mapped (NVML-only tools such as `nvidia-smi` open the same device files but
never load libcuda). Both PID namespaces number processes in creation order, so the pairing is by
order: `*` when the counts match or a process starting while gputaskman runs pins it, `?` when
NVML lists more compute processes than the container has (another container on the same GPU).
Per-process GPU load follows the match. Anything left over is shown as `H:<pid>`,
*outside this container* (for example, the host's display server), and is never looked up locally.

Live check, on a Vast.ai Docker container (Ubuntu 22.04, RTX 3060 Ti, driver 580.82.09): two
PyTorch jobs already running at startup, a third started while watching, and one killed, were all
matched to the right container PIDs with their NVML sizes (1.12, 2.52 and 1.59 GB) and live GPU%.
An Ollama `qwen3:0.6b` runner was detected and named from Ollama's store with `api+mapped+cmdline`
evidence, its weights / KV-cache / compute split shown, and the TUI rendered. Bare-metal Linux
(same PID namespace, no matching needed) is covered by tests but has not been run on hardware.

**AMD GPUs on native Linux** (the `amdgpu` driver) need no ROCm, AMD SMI, or extra package: the
kernel already exposes what's needed.

| | Source |
|---|---|
| Device VRAM, GTT, load, temperature, power, clocks, fan, PCIe link | `/sys/class/drm/card*/device` and its `hwmon` |
| Per-process VRAM and GTT | `drm-resident-vram` / `drm-resident-gtt` (older kernels: `drm-memory-*`) and `drm-shared-*` in `/proc/<pid>/fdinfo/<fd>` |
| Per-process engine load (gfx, compute, video) | `drm-engine-*` busy time, sampled twice (`n/a` until a new client has two samples); `n/a` for ROCm/HIP processes (see below) |

GTT is GPU-accessible system RAM, so it fills the SPILL column (and `shared (in system RAM)` for
the device), like WDDM's non-local usage. On an APU (an integrated GPU, detected by amdgpu not
reporting a VRAM vendor, a heuristic validated on one APU) GTT is the GPU's normal memory and "VRAM"
is only a RAM carve-out, so GTT is still shown but never flagged as spill, and an LLM's memory is its
VRAM plus GTT. The SDMA engine (`dma`) fills the COPY column. Paged stays blank: there is no commit
counter. VRAM and SPILL are charged to a process only when nothing else can hold its bytes: each of
its DRM clients has exactly one visible holder, was opened through a render node (`/dev/dri/renderD*`),
and reports zero bytes in every `drm-shared-*` region. Then its resident VRAM and GTT are its own and add
up without double counting. Otherwise the process shows VRAM and SPILL as `n/a` (`null` in JSON, with
`vram_unattributed_reason`) and its bytes stay in *unattributed*:

- **Shared client** (fd passing, fork; 1Password and its crash handler on the test desktop): one set of
  counters, and nothing says which process uses it. GPU% is `n/a` too.
- **Shared buffers** (a window a compositor imports, video frames): `drm-shared-*` counts a buffer by
  where it *prefers* to live, resident or not, while `drm-resident-*` counts where buffers *are*, so
  resident minus shared is not private memory and is never computed.
- **Primary node** (`/dev/dri/card*`, typically a compositor): root-owned logind keeps a copy of that
  fd, which a normal user can't see, so a single holder can't be proven.
- **Legacy**: older kernels whose amdgpu fdinfo lacks `drm-shared-vram`/`drm-shared-gtt`, and Intel integrated GPUs
  and `xe` (below).
- **Incomplete**: some of the process's fds or fdinfo could not be read (GPU% is `n/a` too).
- **Partial scan**: the TUI's 50 ms listing budget ran out this refresh, so a process it skipped might
  hold the same client (GPU% is `n/a` too). Expected to be rare on a desktop (~9 ms for ~8,000 fds,
  not yet re-measured with this rule); one-shot output always scans fully.

The inspector and JSON (`vram_resident_bytes`, `gtt_resident_bytes`) still show every buffer the
process can reach, shared ones included; the same buffer can appear under several processes, so these
are a reference and are never summed. Unparseable or missing values are unknown (`null`), not 0. amdgpu has no device-wide
video engine counter, so the device's encode/decode load stays N/A; per-process video load is
measured. On VCN 4 and later (RDNA3 and newer, including the RX 9070) decode and encode share one
ring, so it is reported as `video` rather than split. Only processes you can inspect are listed; the header and JSON (`process_status`) say how many could not be, and `sudo` includes other users'. `--gpu 1`
selects the next card, such as an APU's integrated GPU next to a discrete one. A ROCm/HIP process
(tagged `HIP`) has its VRAM in fdinfo like any other. Its GPU% is not: HIP submits compute through user-mode queues on `/dev/kfd`, which the kernel
does not time per process, so a process holding `/dev/kfd` shows engines as `n/a` (`null` in JSON)
rather than a measured-looking 0. The device's `AMD gfx` load does include that work.
This path is native-Linux only; under WSL the GPU is `/dev/dxg`, with no DRM driver involved.

Live check, bare-metal Arch-based Linux (kernel 7.2.15, `amdgpu`), Radeon RX 9070-series (Navi 48)
plus a Radeon 610M iGPU: both cards were found, named, and read; VAAPI HEVC encode and decode with `ffmpeg`
each showed as a `video` row at ~95-100% video load (on the RX 9070 both were charged to amdgpu's
unified `enc` ring, hence `video`); desktop processes' VRAM summed
to less than the card's used VRAM, with the compositor's imported windows listed as shared.
llama.cpp's ROCm server image (`ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-rocm`, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
Q4_K_M, `-ngl 99 -c 8192`, next to a running game) showed as an `LLM` row with `llama.cpp+ggml+HIP`
and 3.95 GB of VRAM, matching the 2.49 GB of weights plus 1.21 GB of f16 KV cache plus compute
buffers, and the 4.11 GB KFD reports for the process in `/sys/class/kfd/kfd/proc/<pid>/vram_*`.
While it generated at 103 tok/s the device read 99% gfx and 339 W, but fdinfo had no engine lines
for it, which is why ROCm rows show engines as `n/a`. PyTorch-ROCm has not been run on this path.
That check predates the stricter attribution above (no subtraction of shared bytes; render-node,
single-holder and complete-scan requirements; per-client timestamps; PID-reuse checks), which is
covered by unit tests only and **not yet validated on AMD hardware**.

**Intel GPUs on native Linux** (the `i915` driver) use the same DRM fdinfo path, with these differences:

| | Source |
|---|---|
| Device temperature, power, GT clock | `hwmon` and `gt/gt0` under `/sys/class/drm/card*`. Power is the rate of the cumulative energy counter between two refreshes, so it is `n/a` on the first |
| Device VRAM total | The size of the local-memory PCI window (`resource2`), an **estimate**: kernel-owned memory is missing from the sysfs view, resizable BAR rounds to a power of two, and a partial window can be smaller than the card, so the total can differ from the card's memory. A window under 1 GiB (an integrated GPU, or a discrete card without resizable BAR) shows `N/A` (`null` in JSON). Free memory is never shown for Intel |
| Device VRAM used | The sum of its clients' resident local memory: i915 has no device-wide counter, so buffers shared between processes can be counted twice, and kernel-owned memory and processes gputaskman can't inspect are missing. The UI, `--once`, `--json` (`memory_note`) and `gputaskman diff` all say so. `n/a` when any client's local memory is unknown |
| Integrated or discrete | An iGPU has no `local0`, so a card with a local-memory window of 1 GiB or more is discrete, and so is any card whose fdinfo reports local memory, even when its window is smaller |
| Per-process VRAM and SPILL | `drm-resident-local0` and `drm-resident-system0`, plus their `stolen-` regions (the firmware-reserved part of each), under the same private-client rules as AMD. `system0` is memory the GPU's buffers currently sit in, including buffers placed there on purpose, so SPILL here (like AMD's GTT) is where they are, not proof they were pushed out of VRAM. Both `drm-shared-local0` and `drm-shared-system0` must be present to charge a process, so an integrated GPU (no `local0`) shows `n/a` (`legacy`). A region value that can't be parsed makes that figure `n/a`, not a smaller number |
| Per-process engine load (3d, compute, copy, video) | `drm-engine-render`, `-compute`, `-copy`, `-video`, `-video-enhance` busy time, sampled twice. `n/a` where the driver reports none (before Gen 8). A class with several identical engines (`drm-engine-capacity-*`, such as video on an Arc) is not divided by its capacity, so one busy engine reads 100% |

Device GPU load, memory bandwidth, and the PCIe link are `n/a`: i915 has no device-wide busy counter, and its
sysfs link fields can report the power-on default instead of the live link. The GT clock is read but not shown yet, and
what is read (`rps_cur_freq_mhz`) is the frequency the driver last *requested*; the kernel's actual frequency is `rps_act_freq_mhz`.
`xe` cards are detected, but its fdinfo uses other keys (`drm-cycles-*`, `drm-resident-vram0`/`-gtt`), so its
per-process rows show `n/a` until they are decoded on hardware.

Live check, reported by the contributor and not repeated by the maintainer: Linux 6.12, an Arc A770 (discrete, 16 GiB
BAR) and a UHD 730 (integrated) on `i915`. Both cards were found, named, and selectable with `--gpu`; the Arc showed
per-process VRAM and engine load, and the TUI rendered both. The fdinfo formats of both drivers, taken from the kernel
sources, are covered by unit tests. **Not validated on hardware:** `xe`, Arc cards without resizable BAR, and
multi-GPU systems other than that pair.

**WSL** is different, because Windows owns the GPU. Linux cannot see how much VRAM its own
processes use: `nvidia-smi` lists no processes, NVML's per-process samples carry *Windows* PIDs
(never looked up in Linux's `/proc`), and Windows charges all Linux GPU memory to the VM worker
process, `vmwp.exe`. When WSL interop is enabled (`/proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc/WSLInterop` reads
`enabled`), gputaskman starts one long-lived `powershell.exe` that reads the Windows GPU counters
through the same PDH array API as the Windows backend and streams them back once a second:

- **WSL VM (`vmwp.exe`)** is the exact total of Linux GPU memory, across every distro, WSLg, and
  Docker Desktop.
- **Windows apps** appear as `W:<pid>` rows with their VRAM, spill, paged, and engine load.
  Windows and Linux PIDs are separate namespaces, so the prefix keeps them apart.
- **Linux rows** get a size by matching `vmwp.exe`'s GPU contexts to Linux processes (below).

The first host sample takes about 2.5 s; the TUI shows `starting` until then, and `--once` waits
for it. The host adapter is paired with the NVML device by memory usage, because WSL's adapter
LUIDs differ from the host's. An ambiguous pairing shows `unmatched` instead of guessing. With other
Hyper-V VMs or Windows Sandbox running, the row is labeled `VM worker` because it cannot be tied
to WSL alone. `--no-host` turns the host stream off; without interop you get device-wide numbers
and a list of the Linux processes that hold `/dev/dxg`, with VRAM shown as `n/a`.

### How WSL per-process VRAM is matched

`vmwp.exe` exposes one GPU-memory instance per guest GPU context, all with the same name: sizes
without owners. Measured on WSL2 with driver 610.88, every Linux process that opens `/dev/dxg`
gets exactly one context (an NVML-only process too, at 0 bytes), and Windows lists them **newest
first**, keeping that order as contexts come and go. Contexts from outside this distro (WSLg, other
distros, Docker, services you cannot inspect) are interleaved by their own age.

gputaskman follows the contexts from sample to sample and labels them with evidence:

| Marker | Meaning | Established by |
|---|---|---|
| `*` matched | Windows' exact size; the owner is inferred, and only one explanation fits (or every one that fits gives the same size) | A new Linux GPU process and a new context appearing together; elimination; this monitor's own context being the only zero-byte candidate at startup; candidate contexts that are exactly the same size |
| `?` guess | Heuristic owner for processes that were already running | Newer process ↔ newer context, outside contexts assumed oldest; cached foreign sizes can rank extra candidates but never establish ownership |
| `n/a` | No context could be assigned | For example, a process that has not created its GPU context yet |

A guess is recomputed every refresh and never counts as evidence for itself. An exited process's
context is held aside until it disappears, so it is not handed to a newcomer, and a context that
grows by gigabytes between refreshes (weights uploading) keeps an established owner. Multiple
zero-byte contexts at startup do not pin the monitor to an arbitrary one that might later grow.
Foreign sizes observed while only the monitor is running are cached per WSL boot in
`~/.cache/gputaskman/`, but remain hints: a process may exit while the monitor is off and a local
process may reuse its size. Observed foreign-context exits and idle samples clear obsolete hints.

The matched size also feeds VRAM sorting, initial model selection, the bounded model-file scan
priority, and the LLM weights / KV-cache breakdown. Inferred Linux rows remain below the VM total
and are never added to it again. The inspector and `--json` (`vram_inferred_by`) say which kind
of match each row has.

In one live check, a 2 GB and a 5 GB PyTorch allocation were matched to the right PIDs at
2.119 GiB and 4.914 GiB: the allocator's own figure plus about 0.26 GiB of CUDA context.
That is one machine and driver, not a guarantee. A process that started long before it first used
the GPU can break the start-order guess, and processes started in the same refresh are ordered by
guess unless their sizes match.

### NixOS

With flakes enabled, run the published flake or a checkout:

```bash
nix run github:shanselman/gputaskman
nix run github:shanselman/gputaskman -- --list-gpus
nix run path:. -- --once
nix run path:. -- --json
```

Build both `gputaskman` and its `gtm` alias with `nix build path:.` (executables are in
`result/bin/`). The flake provides packages for `x86_64-linux` and `aarch64-linux`; `flake.lock`
pins nixpkgs. Dependencies come from nixpkgs, independently of `uv.lock`. No pip installation,
virtual environment, CUDA Toolkit, or ROCm installation is needed. GPU drivers remain supplied by
the host, never bundled with the package. NVIDIA's nixpkgs Python binding finds NVML through
`/run/opengl-driver/lib`; AMD and Intel use kernel sysfs and DRM fdinfo interfaces directly. On WSL2 the
host driver lives in `/usr/lib/wsl/lib` instead, and the wrappers add that directory to
`LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (it is ignored when absent, so NixOS is unaffected).

For source development and tests:

```bash
nix develop path:.
python -m gputaskman --once
python -m unittest discover -s tests -q
```

`nix flake check path:.` builds the package and runs the same hardware-independent tests.
For a flake-based NixOS configuration, add this repository as a `gputaskman` input, then include
`inputs.gputaskman.packages.${pkgs.stdenv.hostPlatform.system}.default` in
`environment.systemPackages`. Enable your GPU's normal NixOS driver configuration first.
The flake was contributed and checked on x86_64 NixOS 26.05; CI does not build it, and ARM64 has
not been validated.

## macOS (Apple Silicon)

Run from a clone (`uv run gputaskman`); there is no portable macOS download yet. Apple GPUs share
one pool of memory with the CPU, so there is no VRAM to split and no spill/commit counters. What
macOS exposes without root:

| Column | Source | Who |
|---|---|---|
| GPU memory (header) | IOAccelerator `PerformanceStatistics`: `Alloc system memory` (all GPU allocations) out of physical RAM | device |
| GPU% (header) | `Device Utilization %` | device |
| GPU% | Each Metal client (`AGXDeviceUserClient`) names its creator PID and keeps a cumulative `accumulatedGPUTime`; the rate between samples, per client (a closed client never hides the others' work) | every process |
| VRAM | `footprint`: the process's memory macOS charges to graphics (the `(graphics)` categories: Metal buffers, textures) | your own processes |
| Runtime, model files | Mapped files from `proc_pidinfo` region walks (psutil has no memory maps on macOS): `libggml*.dylib`, `libllama*.dylib`, `libmlx*.dylib`, `libtorch_cpu.dylib`, the Metal driver bundle | your own processes |

Other users' processes (WindowServer, system daemons) show GPU% with memory `n/a`: `footprint` needs
root for them. Idle ones are left out of the table, except WindowServer. Run with `sudo` to measure
every process's memory. `footprint` takes ~70 ms per process, so it runs in a background thread:
busy processes and new ones every pass (~2 s), idle ones every 30 s. A new process shows `n/a` for a
second or two until its first measurement; a single failed measurement keeps the last size, and three
in a row back off for a minute. Measurements are tied to the process's start time, so a reused PID
never shows the previous process's numbers.

Metal reports one GPU time per process, with no 3D/compute/copy/video split, so those columns show
`n/a`; a Metal process above 10% GPU is classified `3D/game` unless something more specific applies
(AI runtime, browser, compositor). Spill, paged, clocks, power, and temperature are not available, so
the chart picker offers only GPU and GPU memory. Handy's log is read from
`~/Library/Logs/com.pais.handy/handy.log`.

Live check on an M4 Mac mini (macOS 26.3.1): a PyTorch MPS job with a 2 GiB buffer and a matmul loop
showed `Python  AI  PyTorch+Metal  3.06 GB  99%`, with device utilization at 99% and allocated GPU
memory rising by the same amount.

Scans skip other apps' sandbox containers (`~/Library/Containers`, `~/Library/Group Containers`) and
system files without opening them: opening a file in a protected container blocks while macOS waits
for a privacy consent prompt.

## What you get

- **Device view:** VRAM usage, GPU activity, memory activity, PCIe traffic, temperature, power,
  video-engine clock, and responsive history charts with an all-charts or single-metric view.
- **Process view:** local GPU memory, GPU-accessible system RAM, estimated non-resident commit,
  engine activity, and detected runtimes such as CUDA, HIP, Vulkan, Direct3D, ggml and ONNX Runtime.
- **Model inspector:** which model each process holds (LLM, decision, embedding, speech, or diffusion), how
  it was identified, architecture, quantization, layer count, weights, estimated KV cost, and
  buffer sizes from compatible load logs.
- **Live server hints:** context size, busy slots, throughput when available, and friendly Ollama
  or LM Studio model names.
- **Scriptable output:** one-shot text and JSON, using the same collector as the TUI.

## Usage

```powershell
uv run --locked gputaskman              # live TUI
uv run --locked gtm                     # shorter alias
uv run --locked gputaskman -i 2         # sample every two seconds
uv run --locked gputaskman --once       # one text snapshot
uv run --locked gputaskman --json       # one JSON snapshot; implies --once
uv run --locked gputaskman diff before.json after.json   # compare two --json snapshots
uv run --locked gputaskman --no-host    # WSL: don't read Windows host counters through interop
uv run --locked gputaskman --help
```

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| Up / Down | Select a process and inspect it |
| `s` | Cycle sort: VRAM, GPU%, spill, paged, name |
| `c` | Cycle all charts or a single metric (also available in the **Charts** dropdown) |
| `a` | Switch between top and all collected processes |
| `m` | Toggle full diagnostics / slim monitoring |
| `p` | Pause / resume collection |
| `?` | Explain the counters and their limits |
| Escape | Close help |
| `q` | Quit |

A wide terminal (roughly 140 columns or more) makes the full table easier to read.
The TUI starts in **Full diagnostics** mode. Press `m` (or click **Slim/Full** in the
footer) for **Slim monitoring**: each GPU header hides driver/CUDA versions, PCI bus
address, driver model, PCIe generation/width, compute capability, power/clock limits,
performance state, and secondary memory/video clocks. GPU identity, memory bars and
provenance/availability warnings, utilization, PCIe throughput, temperature, current power
and SM/GFX clock, throttling alerts, charts, processes, and process inspection remain.
The header border names the active mode; press `m` again to restore the full details.
This is a session-only display toggle, applies to every GPU, and does not change collection
or one-shot text/JSON output.
All eight history charts are shown by default: GPU, SM clock (GFX clock on AMD), VRAM, memory activity,
temperature, power, encoder, and decoder. They stack in narrow terminals and share rows as
the window widens. Click the **Charts** dropdown to focus on one metric or return to **All charts**.
A blank sample means no reading; zero is drawn at the baseline. Percentages use a 0–100%
scale, temperature uses 0–120°C, and the power and clock scales are displayed below the charts.
The dashboard and inspector scroll independently in short terminals so the process list stays usable.
Model/runtime discovery is throttled, so newly loaded models may take about 15 seconds to appear.

On multi-GPU systems, the TUI stacks a header and trend charts for each GPU and adds a **GPU**
column to the combined process list. A process using two GPUs has a separate row for each;
selecting a row inspects its memory on that GPU. Single-GPU layouts are unchanged.
Memory totals and histories stay separate per device; model files and runtime buffer logs
can span devices and do not prove per-device model placement. Discovery's 150 ms scan budget
is divided across GPUs, though each GPU has its own counter and telemetry queries.
This layout is covered by synthetic tests, **not yet validated on multi-GPU hardware**.
On Windows, the live TUI checks DXGI adapter topology every five seconds in the existing
sampling worker (or on the next sample with a longer interval). Removed adapters retain their
session GPU number with unavailable readings; surviving adapters keep their collectors and
histories, and newly discovered adapters are appended. Re-enabling an adapter rebuilds its
providers. LUIDs identify adapters; if a LUID changes, only a unique PCI location **and**
matching vendor/description can reconnect the old slot. Without that evidence, the old slot
remains unavailable rather than transferring its history or process ownership to another GPU.
`--gpu N` pins the adapter selected at startup, not whichever adapter later occupies index N;
it does not start monitoring other newly discovered devices. Session GPU numbers therefore
need not match a fresh `--list-gpus` after a topology change.
NVML handles are reacquired at the same low-frequency cadence; missing counters, lost telemetry
or sampling errors trigger provider reconstruction at the next successful discovery. Persistent
failures back off to at most one reconstruction per minute; a reappearing or changed adapter retries immediately.
Discovery errors retain the last known topology with a warning, not invented zero usage.
Pausing suspends discovery as well as sampling; resume performs an overdue check.
This recovery is covered by mocks, **not validated with hardware disable/re-enable** on the
reporter's hybrid AMD/NVIDIA laptop. On a three-GPU desktop (RTX 5060 Ti, RTX 3060, AMD iGPU;
Windows 11 build 26200, NVIDIA driver 610.88), disabling and re-enabling the RTX 3060 recovered
its slot, history, VRAM and processes, but NVML reads for that GPU then faulted inside `nvml.dll`
and `nvmlShutdown()` hung on exit. A fresh process read it normally. gputaskman therefore stops
reading NVML for a GPU whose reads fault, shows "restart gputaskman to restore it", and skips
`nvmlShutdown()` once an NVIDIA adapter has gone away (process exit releases the session). That
mitigation is covered by mocks and not yet validated on that hardware. It is not a claim of
physical hot-swap support.
Other backends and one-shot output retain startup-only discovery.
Under multi-GPU WSL, host attribution is disabled with a reason rather than risking matching
two devices by memory usage; Linux processes are listed once with GPU `?`, because `/dev/dxg`
does not identify their GPU. `--gpu N` retains the existing single-device host matching.

`--list-gpus` lists selectable hardware adapters with their vendor and LUID. `--gpu N` selects
one of these adapters: NVIDIA adapters are listed first, followed by other vendors, with each
group ordered by dedicated memory. An out-of-range
index is rejected rather than silently selecting another device. Compute-only devices such as an
NPU are not graphics adapters. AMD and NVIDIA hardware coverage is described below; configurations
with multiple GPUs and mixed vendors need further hardware validation. `--once` and `--json`
still default to GPU 0; use `--gpu N` to collect another device without changing the snapshot format.
Device telemetry is matched to WDDM adapters by PCI location, not display name or enumeration order.
If a unique match cannot be established, telemetry is unavailable; buffer logs can still span devices,
so model-buffer attribution across GPUs is not yet reliable. This conservative matching also applies
to NVIDIA and may suppress telemetry when Windows does not expose a usable PCI address.

AMD adapters can be selected and use the existing Windows GPU process counters; HIP runtime DLLs
are recognized as runtime evidence. On supported drivers, the AMD Display Library supplied by the
Windows driver can provide graphics activity, clocks, edge temperature, board or ASIC power, fan
and PCIe lane count. An optional AMD SMI Python installation is a fallback and may provide graphics
activity, edge temperature and socket power. Both require a PCI match to the selected WDDM adapter.
The SMI library and its native dependencies must be available to the Python environment; it is not
bundled in the portable build. The RX 9060 XT HIP workload and ADL telemetry have been observed on
this machine; AMD SMI telemetry and Vulkan workloads remain unvalidated.
A loaded DLL does not prove GPU execution.

Unavailable utilization, temperature, power, clock and PCIe readings are displayed as `N/A` in
text and the TUI and as `null` in JSON. For example, a missing NVML power limit means that the
driver did not expose that reading; it does not by itself indicate a hardware fault.
Missing per-process memory or engine samples likewise show `N/A`/`null`; the paged estimate is
unavailable when any of its input counters is missing.

On GPU-paravirtualized VMs, including Windows Sandbox, Windows may expose GPU counter LUIDs that
do not match the selected DXGI adapter. When that happens, the counters cannot safely be assigned
to the adapter: the process list and usage are unavailable, not zero. The text and TUI explain
the mismatch; JSON reports it in `counter_status` and sets `counter_adapter_matched` to `false`
(`null` when the check does not apply).
GPU-PV guests may also omit adapter memory counters. Counter values that are actually reported as
zero remain zero; a zero alone does not establish that a counter is unavailable.

Live check: Windows Sandbox on Windows 11 build 26100, hosted by an RTX 4080 SUPER with NVIDIA
driver 630.20. `D3DKMTEnumAdapters2/3` exposed the PDH LUID `0x4BF1` as a software adapter with a
different adapter/render GUID from DXGI's `0x4BB7`; it was not a proven alias for the NVIDIA GPU.
The portable build's `--once` explanation and `--json` unmatched status were verified in the guest.
Other Hyper-V GPU-PV configurations have not been validated.

### Comparing snapshots

To see which memory bucket actually grew when you load a model or change the context length, save
a JSON snapshot before and after and compare them:

```powershell
uv run --locked gputaskman --json > before.json
# load the model, or restart the server with a different -c, then send it one request
uv run --locked gputaskman --json > after.json
uv run --locked gputaskman diff before.json after.json          # add --json for machine-readable output
```

The device and process tables compare **measured** counters only. Runtime-reported segments
(llama.cpp buffer logs) and estimates (KV cache from GGUF metadata and `-c`) are listed separately
under each process and are never added to measured totals. A model file that appears in a process
is listed as evidence that the process opened or named it, not as GPU growth.

Processes are paired by PID, then by name and listening ports, then by a unique name, because a
model reload often restarts the server under a new PID. A process missing from one snapshot shows
`not listed`, not zero: it was not running or used too little GPU to be listed. Processes that
moved by less than 16 MB are hidden from the text output but included in `--json`.

Take the "after" snapshot once the model has answered one request: CUDA and Vulkan can allocate
lazily, and allocators keep freed memory cached, so shrinkage may appear late. On an RTX 4080 SUPER
with Docker Model Runner's llama-server (Vulkan) and gemma-3-270m, changing `-c 4096` to `-c 32768`
estimated +504 MB of KV cache, but the server's measured dedicated memory grew by only +83 MB.
Gemma 3 uses sliding-window attention, so the estimate is an upper bound. The comparison makes
that gap visible instead of hiding it.

## How can it know what's inside?

It combines evidence rather than reading arbitrary GPU memory. Windows' graphics kernel supplies
per-process memory and engine counters, while NVML or AMD ADL/SMI supplies device metrics. Process DLLs suggest
the runtime, and mapped files or command-line arguments identify candidate models. GGUF metadata
and tensor offsets let it estimate weights and KV-cache costs; compatible runtime logs and local
server APIs add allocated buffer sizes and live state. That can explain a llama.cpp process well,
but a runtime DLL or filename alone does not prove which allocation contains which object.

| Question | Evidence | Confidence / limitation |
|---|---|---|
| How full and busy is the card? | WDDM adapter counters and NVML or AMD ADL/SMI | Measured; driver support varies by metric |
| Which process uses GPU memory? | WDDM process counters; NVML on Linux | Measured accounting, not a resource ownership graph |
| Which WSL process uses GPU memory? | Windows host counters for `vmwp.exe`, matched to Linux processes | Exact VM total; per-process owner inferred (`*`) or guessed (`?`) |
| Which engines are active? | WDDM engine counters | CUDA can appear on the **3D** engine |
| Which runtime is loaded? | Mapped DLL names | Detection, not proof that every library is doing GPU work |
| Which model file is present? | Mapped files, CLI flags, GGUF magic/header | A file mapping does not prove GPU placement |
| Weights / KV / compute sizes? | Load logs, GGUF math, server state | Log-reported allocations or estimates, not a VRAM scan |
| Which texture, tensor, or kernel is this? | Not available here | Use PIX, Nsight, or runtime-specific instrumentation |

### Why not just `nvidia-smi`?

On GeForce under **WDDM**, Windows manages GPU memory and NVML may report per-process memory as
`N/A`. Windows GPU counters can still attribute memory and activity across Direct3D, Vulkan,
OpenGL, and CUDA. NVML remains useful for device-level readings. Under WSL, `nvidia-smi` lists
no processes at all; see [Linux and WSL](#linu

items.title: voyager-so/vork
items.description: Headless 3D and VFX engine for agents. Research preview.
items.readme: **vork is a 3D and VFX engine built for AI agents.** Agents write the whole scene as code, including their own shaders, materials, cameras and physics, and vork renders it on the GPU. The core API fits in about 2,500 tokens. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/03cfa020-be40-483a-89af-1ef77467b7a0 **One million birds, each on its own path.** 192 frames at 1080p rendered in 97 seconds on a single NVIDIA L4. Blender EEVEE at the same sample count is projected at 13–18 minutes. [How we measured](#million-birds-measured-movies-projected-blender-times) · [how it's made](examples/murmuration/) · [credits](examples/murmuration/CREDITS) - **Built for agents:** a small API that agents can extend with their own GPU programs. - **Fast:** 1.1–2.3× faster than EEVEE on default stills and movies, and about 8–11× on the bird flock. [Speed, with the qualifications](#speed-with-the-qualifications). - **Native GPU engine:** written in Rust and Slang, runs on Vulkan and Metal (Linux, Windows, macOS). ## Paste this to your agent [Install vork](#install), then paste: > Run `vork init my-shot`, read `vork help`, render a preview and inspect the image. > Refine the camera and lighting before rendering at final quality. Read the > relevant help topic when you need a feature the first page doesn't explain. vork is written in Rust and Slang, with GPU rendering through Vulkan and Metal. An agent writes a scene, renders it, looks at the result and revises the code. There is no editor to drive. Most creative tools expose controls that a person can operate. An agent can also write a shader in the middle of a shot. vork gives it geometry, ray queries and GPU execution, then lets scene programs define materials, cameras, light propagation, simulation and compositing. Ordinary shots need only scene data; the programming hooks are there when the shot needs something unusual. Source-available and free during the research preview. ## Start here After [installing vork](#install), create a working project: ```sh vork init my-shot cd my-shot vork render scene.json --out render.png vork help ``` Open `render.png`, change a colour or camera position in `scene.json`, and render again. The starter uses only bundled sphere, box and grid primitives: no downloads, no GPU needed to initialize. Use `vork init my-shot --language typescript` or `--language python` for editable `scene.ts` or `scene.py` alongside the ready-to-render JSON. The generated README explains regeneration and SDK requirements. Existing files are never overwritten. The default `std/final` profile is warmed by setup; use `--profile std/draft` for quicker previews. ## What you can make The examples include code, preparation commands and credits. Large downloaded assets and footage stay outside Git; the recipes fetch them or accept a local path. The images here are stills from these shots. Keep each credit with its image. ### [Million birds](examples/murmuration/) ![A ribbon of starlings crossing the low sun above a lagoon](docs/images/birds-sun-ribbon.jpg) | | | |---|---| | ![A foreground bird above the flock at dusk](docs/images/birds-skim.jpg) | ![The flock curving over still water, seen from above](docs/images/birds-lagoon.jpg) | A million simulated agents steered by Slang compute programs, with a camera skimming through the flock. The camera and nine foreground birds are authored; the simulated million do not flap. The bird stills above come from the measured four-sample, denoised skim and reveal movies. Credit: based on ["Crow"](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/crow-d5a9b0df4da3493688b63ce42c8a83e2) by Alexei Ostapenko, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes: sampled flight pose, reduced distant mesh, rescaled, articulated flight wings, extracted wings for the starling body, resized textures. [All bird and environment credits](examples/murmuration/CREDITS). ### [Cyber car](https://voyager.so/vork) [![A cyber car on a mountain road at sunset — watch the film](https://cdn.moda.app/voyager/blog/vork/cyber-car-poster-2f939652f3e77c3c.webp)](https://voyager.so/vork) [Watch the film](https://voyager.so/vork): a car drives into the night as the forest turns into glowing cyan wireframe, drawn from real triangle edges by a scene shader. Credit: [“Car Concept”](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF-Sample-Assets/tree/main/Models/CarConcept) by Unity Fan, glTF adaptation by Eric Chadwick / Darmstadt Graphics Group, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes: scaled, animated, brighter head and tail lights, wheel pose. Trees, ground and asphalt from Poly Haven (CC0). The far mountains and sky are an image-model painting on a curved 3D card; everything else that moves is rendered. ### [VFX on real footage](examples/vfx-artifact/) | Original footage | Tracked camera and proxy geometry | Final look | |---|---|---| | ![The photographed take: a woman asleep at a laptop](docs/images/seed-1-original.jpg) | ![Proxy geometry over the same take](docs/images/seed-2-tracked.jpg) | ![A glowing seed on the desk, with the room relit to night](docs/images/seed-3-final.jpg) | A procedural ceramic-and-bronze seed, a tracked camera, occlusion mattes and proxy geometry for relighting. The example teaches the base composite; the final look adds later relighting and wipes. Real footage + rendered 3D; no generative video. Credit: footage by **Ron Lach / Pexels**, modified under the Pexels Licence. Original performer; no endorsement implied. [Source and preparation](examples/vfx-artifact/). ### [After Rain](examples/vfx-neon/) ![A glowing cyan sculpture and an AFTER RAIN sign in a wet night alley, reflected in a puddle](docs/images/after-rain.jpg) A suspended neon seed and blade sign added to a moving shot of an empty alley at night, with spill on the wall and reflections in the wet street. Real footage + rendered 3D; no generative video. Credit: footage is ["Ally"](https://www.pexels.com/video/ally-18972999/) by **Rafael Fernanz / Pexels**, modified under the [Pexels Licence](https://www.pexels.com/license/). [Source and preparation](examples/vfx-neon/). ### [Black hole](examples/black-hole/) ![A cargo ship beside a black hole, with a moon lensed into a ring around it](docs/images/black-hole.jpg) The scene supplies a Schwarzschild light-propagation program through vork's public hook. Curved paths, capture and the disk's appearance live in the example. It is a numerical approximation, not an exact relativistic solver. Credit: based on ["Corinth Cargo Transporter"](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/corinth-cargo-transporter-7614d85856f6477ba2a603970dcbb0dd) by [Yvo Pors](https://sketchfab.com/yvopors14), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes: decimated geometry, resized, compressed and exposure-adjusted textures, adjusted material roughness and metallic weight, placement and scale. [Ship credit](examples/black-hole/README.md#ship-credit). ### [Cake](examples/cake/) ![A carrot cake on a carved plate, with a kettle out of focus behind it](docs/images/cake.jpg) A moving camera, depth of field and daylight on detailed scanned assets. This shot is rendered 3D, using Poly Haven assets; it isn't a photographed take. Credit: Poly Haven CC0 assets; carrot cake photography by Greg Zaal, processing by James Ray Cock. [Full cake credits](examples/cake/CREDITS.md). ### [Cozy Kitchen](examples/kitchen/) ![A miniature kitchen diorama with pumpkins on the roof](docs/images/kitchen.jpg) Nicole Morena's Blender 3.5 splash scene, imported into vork. The recipe uses a shared material adaptation and a camera orbit; the pictured render has additional staging and animated lighting. Credit: **Cozy Kitchen** by [Nicole Morena](https://www.artstation.com/nickyblender), [source .blend](https://download.blender.org/demo/splash/blender-3.5-splash.blend), [CC BY-SA](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/) (version unspecified by source). Adapted and rendered in vork: camera orbit, animated lighting, widescreen framing, material translation and staging changes. This still and the adapted animation are shared under CC BY-SA. No artist endorsement implied. [Changes and share-alike notice](examples/kitchen/CREDITS.md). ### [Water](examples/water/) ![Water splashing up in a crown from a white basin on a wooden deck](docs/images/water.jpg) A GPU liquid simulation implemented as Slang compute programs in vork's fluid library. It uses published APIC/FLIP and surface-reconstruction methods, with an authored initial impulse and limited secondary spray. ## No suitable GPU? Rendering requires Apple Silicon or an NVIDIA GPU with Vulkan ray queries. Scene authoring and `vork help` work without a GPU. On your own NVIDIA Linux machine, you can use the [Docker runtime](docs/REMOTE-GPU.md). ## Give it to an agent Start with `vork init`, then `vork help`. Scene JSON uses the stable [editor schema](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/voyager-so/vork/v0.3.0/packages/ts/scene.schema.json). Use `vork help` for the starting scene and concepts, `vork help TOPIC --all` for topic fields, and `vork help field PATH` for an exact field reference. Use the [prompt above](#paste-this-to-your-agent) to start. Python and TypeScript can author ordinary scene JSON through the SDKs. You can also write JSON directly. For example, save this as `scene.json` (also available as [examples/first-scene.json](examples/first-scene.json)): ```json {"version":2,"nodes":[ {"type":"mesh","geometry":{"std":"sphere","radius":1}, "materials":[{"inputs":{"base_color":[0.12,0.35,0.65],"specular_roughness":0.3}}]}, {"type":"mesh","translation":[0,-1,0],"geometry":{"std":"grid","size":[10,10]}, "materials":[{"inputs":{"base_color":[0.35,0.35,0.35]}}]}, {"type":"light","shape":"rectangle","translation":[-3,5,4],"target":[0,0,0], "energy":700,"size":4,"color":[1,0.92,0.8]}, {"type":"camera","translation":[3,2,5],"target":[0,0,0]} ],"render":{"resolution":[640,480]}} ``` ```sh vork render scene.json --profile std/previs --out preview.png vork render scene.json --profile std/final --out final.png vork help sdk vork help programs --all ``` Scene content and render quality are separate. Use `std/previs` to iterate, `std/draft` for scene-ray lighting at 4 samples, `std/final` for the default delivery profile, and `std/path` for path transport.
