Final approximates indirect lighting and can darken interiors, including glossy bounces. More samples do not restore omitted transport; try path and inspect. Draft and final use 4 and 8 samples with bundled OIDN denoising by default; use `--set denoise=false` to turn it off. `--set samples=N` overrides the profile budget (1..4096); more samples means cleaner and slower. Without a fast GPU denoiser (NVIDIA or Apple GPU), draft and final say so and use 16 and 32 samples undenoised; `--set denoise=true` runs the slow CPU denoiser anyway. For a particular field, ask `vork help field node.target`. Help topics include exact fields with `--all`. Images, video and control passes come from the same scene; see `vork help outputs`. ## Under the hood Default rendering combines raster visibility with hardware ray-traced lighting; a path tracer is also available. The scene and render plan stay installed. Frames use retained GPU resources, with GPU-to-hardware-video encoding on supported native paths. A portable encoding fallback reads pixels back to the CPU. Slang programs run on the GPU. Host parsing, planning, animation-track evaluation and IO still use the CPU. The public program hooks let a scene author change camera rays, material response, light propagation and film response without editing the renderer. `vork help programs --all` describes their scope. Validation includes furnace tests and analytic oracles, alongside render tests. That is a way to catch errors, not a guarantee that every scene is physically exact. ## Speed, with the qualifications These are timings, **not equal-quality speedups**. The draft/final results come from the build identified by SHA-256 in the results report on an NVIDIA L4: final uses eight samples and OIDN, draft four and OIDN. All 152 planned jobs were accounted for. The broader sweep delivered 583 of 585 images; the million-stars stress scene ran out of GPU memory in both profiles. Visual review found softer edges, grainier defocus, wall mottling and changed sparse or spectral highlights at these budgets. Nineteen earlier quality comparisons failed their declared no-worse FLIP condition; that experiment was not repeated for this build. vork times below are complete command wall times, including startup, scene loading, output writes and encoding. Setup, shader warmup, provisioning and transfers are excluded. Stills use five warm repetitions, movies three. Driver caches and clocks were not controlled. Blender 5.2.1 times are retained measured baselines, not fresh runs: EEVEE uses different settings, and its movie times exclude startup/loading after a still prime. Both movie timings include encoding. The car is a proxy. [Benchmark method and recorded results](benchmarks/RESULTS.md) explain the boundaries and carried-forward numbers. ### Default final: stills 1080p PNG, seconds. EEVEE uses 64 samples without denoising; vork uses eight with OIDN. Missing Blender results are unmeasured, not wins. | Scene input | EEVEE (s) | vork final (s) | Comparison | |---|---:|---:|---| | [B-push-in.json](benchmarks/B-push-in.json) | 2.912 | 1.993 | 1.46× faster | | [B-turntable.json](benchmarks/B-turntable.json) | 3.148 | 2.247 | 1.40× faster | | [B-walking.json](benchmarks/B-walking.json) | 2.612 | 1.890 | 1.38× faster | | [B-interior.json](benchmarks/B-interior.json) | 2.892 | 1.738 | 1.66× faster | | [B-street.json](benchmarks/B-street.json) | unmeasured | 2.043 | unmeasured | | [B-rack-focus.json](benchmarks/B-rack-focus.json) | unmeasured | 1.787 | unmeasured | | [B-car-pan.json](benchmarks/B-car-pan.json) | 2.458 | 1.691 | 1.45× faster | | [B-crowd.json](benchmarks/B-crowd.json) | unmeasured | 2.046 | unmeasured | | [B-night.json](benchmarks/B-night.json) | 2.963 | 1.937 | 1.53× faster | ### Default final: complete movies 240 frames, 1920×1080, 24 fps. These four public B-scene clips are part of the seven-scene comparison; the full seven measured 1.14–2.32× against EEVEE. Different quality and timing boundaries still apply. | Scene input | EEVEE (s) | vork final (s) | Comparison | |---|---:|---:|---| | [B-blocking.json](benchmarks/B-blocking.json) | 88.072 | 47.082 | 1.87× faster | | [B-interior.json](benchmarks/B-interior.json) | 107.026 | 59.231 | 1.81× faster | | [B-car-pan.json](benchmarks/B-car-pan.json) | 93.489 | 81.740 | 1.14× faster | | [B-night.json](benchmarks/B-night.json) | 213.477 | 92.201 | 2.32× faster | ### Path tracing: carried-forward measurements These 1080p still timings were measured in an earlier build, rather than the measured final build. Adaptive sampling up to 4,096, threshold 0.01, minimum 64; stopping implementations differ. vork is slower in both cases below. | Scene input | Cycles (s) | vork path (s) | Comparison | |---|---:|---:|---| | [B-car-pan.json](benchmarks/B-car-pan.json) | 4.632 | 26.901 | 5.81× slower | | [B-night.json](benchmarks/B-night.json) | 16.041 | 31.860 | 1.99× slower | ### Setup and first use On [B-blocking.json](benchmarks/B-blocking.json), the final-profile setup took 250.792 s, the first still after setup 2.298 s, and the warm median 2.094 s. The retained EEVEE cold still was 20.633 s and warm median 2.405 s. Other scenes can still spend substantial time compiling new programs after setup: rack-focus's first final still took 82.057 s, versus its 1.787 s warm median. ### Previews: carried-forward measurements These are earlier-build `std/previs` results, not measured on the final build identified in [RESULTS.md](benchmarks/RESULTS.md). Previews use different lighting and shadows; these are not final-quality comparisons. Complete 240-frame, 1080p24 movies, median of three warm commands: | Scene input | Preview movie (s) | |---|---:| | [B-blocking.json](benchmarks/B-blocking.json) | 3.496 | | [B-interior.json](benchmarks/B-interior.json) | 4.565 | | [B-car-pan.json](benchmarks/B-car-pan.json) | 6.391 | | [B-night.json](benchmarks/B-night.json) | 5.864 | | [B-crowd.json](benchmarks/B-crowd.json) | 4.097 | | [B-push-in.json](benchmarks/B-push-in.json) | 3.705 | | [B-rack-focus.json](benchmarks/B-rack-focus.json) | 3.902 | | [B-street.json](benchmarks/B-street.json) | 3.964 | | [B-turntable.json](benchmarks/B-turntable.json) | 4.612 | | [B-walking.json](benchmarks/B-walking.json) | 2.190 | Across the seven simple preview clips on that earlier build, EEVEE/vork was 14.63–36.40× and Workbench/vork 3.99–11.24×. Those ranges use retained Blender baselines and different rendering settings and timing boundaries. They do not describe default final rendering. ### Million birds: measured movies, projected Blender times The [bird inputs](benchmarks/birds/README.md) include the compute programs and all three cameras. These `std/draft` movies use four samples and OIDN at 1080p24; each number is the median of three full commands. The first full movie is included in that three-command median, after a separate 320×180 still warmup. Setup and warmup are excluded from the movie times below. For skim, setup + warmup + the movie median total 506.781 seconds (8.45 minutes); asset preparation and transfers are additional. | Camera input | Frames | vork movie (s) | Setup (s) | Warmup (s) | EEVEE 16-sample projection (s), both retained runs | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | [skim.json.in](benchmarks/birds/skim.json.in) | 192 | 96.942 | 243.809 | 166.030 | 1511.108 / 1817.625 | | [dive.json.in](benchmarks/birds/dive.json.in) | 240 | 124.718 | 167.376 | 112.994 | 2517.891 / 2417.831 | | [reveal.json.in](benchmarks/birds/reveal.json.in) | 288 | 153.411 | 163.218 | 113.910 | 2916.237 / 2889.758 | The EEVEE values extrapolate eight warm frames; they are **projections, not measured movies**. They omit simulation, startup and video encoding, and receive the finished flock as geometry. They use **16 samples** against vork's four, so this table is not a like-for-like speed comparison. The matching four-sample EEVEE projection exists only for skim: 773.7–1,082.5 s across the retained runs, with ray tracing on or off, about 8–11× the 96.9 s vork movie. Dive and reveal have no four-sample EEVEE projection. Quality, material translation and motion differ. ### Rerun ```sh python3 benchmarks/fetch.py python3 benchmarks/run.py --vork vork --out /tmp/vork-benchmark python3 integrations/blender/benchmark.py --blender blender --out /tmp/blender-benchmark ``` The vork runner measures undenoised B-scene variants, not the denoised final8 tables above. It omits draft and does not set the recorded seed 11. The bird runner uses previs/final with a full-resolution warmup, not the recorded draft4 workflow. The final8/draft4 tables use build `81ae2b075`; preview and path results come from earlier freezes, as noted beside those tables. The Blender helper has been checked for preparation of all ten scenes on Blender 5.2.1. The historical GPU timing comparisons have not been rerun with this repair; see [the method](benchmarks/README.md). ## Research-preview limits Participating media (fog, haze, smoke and volumes) are unsupported in 0.3. Used medium bindings and volume topology are refused; removed programs such as `std/fog` fail lookup even in unused definitions. Bake an image plate and composite it, or render the medium externally. For a deliberately dry alternative, remove medium-only nodes, bindings and definitions while preserving shared surfaces. See `vork help upgrade` and `vork help limits`. Large scenes and dense transparency can fail, including on Mac; reducing image resolution alone does not necessarily fix them. Some heavy interiors work with `std/path` when the default hybrid profile fails. First use of a new program can involve substantial compilation, even after `vork setup`. At four/eight samples, fine facades and hair can lose detail, defocus can show stepped or grainy edges, and sparse sparks or spectral highlights can change brightness and colour. Try `--set samples=32` for these shots; more samples cost more time. The frozen sweep retained a million-stars allocation failure in both profiles. Mac reliability was not revalidated in that Linux run. The water quickstart is a closed-shutter diagnostic. The full motion-blurred scene is much more expensive. It is a uniform-grid experiment with finite particle budgets, unresolved thin features and no two-way rigid-body coupling. It is not a general replacement for a mature simulation package. The VFX camera solve and single-view relief are estimates, with limitations documented beside the example. Fog returns in 0.4 with a design independent of pause/resume. Broader simulation, reliability and performance on demanding scenes remain future directions, without promised release dates. Read `vork help limits` before committing to a shot. ## Install Upgrading scenes or scripts? Run `vork help upgrade` ([upgrade guide](docs/help/upgrade.md)). Binary packages are available from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/voyager-so/vork/releases) for Linux, Windows and Mac. Keep the entire install folder together: Slang, OIDN, libraries, examples, SDKs and licence texts are runtime companions to the binary. - **Linux:** x64, glibc 2.35+ and libstdc++ with `GLIBCXX_3.4.30` (Ubuntu 22.04+), a recent NVIDIA GPU and its hardware-ray-tracing Vulkan driver. - **Windows:** x64 Windows 10/11, a recent NVIDIA GPU and its hardware-ray-tracing Vulkan driver. - **Mac:** Apple Silicon with Metal, macOS 26 for the bundled Slang toolchain. Older macOS versions are unqualified. Intel Macs are unsupported. H.264 uses system VideoToolbox. For TypeScript authoring, install **Node 22.18+** (with npm) from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/en/download). For Python authoring, install **Python 3.11+** from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/) or your platform's package manager. These runtimes are not bundled and are not needed for JSON scenes. Ubuntu 22.04's default Python 3.10 and Node packages are too old. On Ubuntu, install `python3-venv` for the distribution's Python, or the matching versioned venv package for your chosen Python (for example `python3.12-venv`). Use that Python 3.11+ executable in the commands below. Minimal Linux images also need `xz-utils` to unpack Node's `.tar.xz` download. ### Linux Install the NVIDIA driver for your GPU first. On Ubuntu 22.04+: ```sh sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl tar libvulkan1 libgomp1 ffmpeg curl -fL https://github.com/voyager-so/vork/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o /tmp/vork-install.sh sh /tmp/vork-install.sh export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" vork --version vork help ``` These dependency commands are for Ubuntu with sudo. In a root container, omit `sudo`; without administrator access, arrange for the dependencies to be installed. The installer itself runs in your user account without root. The installer verifies SHA256SUMS, installs under `$HOME/.local/lib/vork`, links `$HOME/.local/bin/vork`, runs `vork setup`, and adds the PATH line to your shell's startup files, including the one login shells read. The `export` above covers the current shell, and any shell that reads no startup file, such as plain `bash -c`. `VORK_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` or a custom `PREFIX` leaves startup files alone. Linux MP4 needs ffmpeg even when NVENC encodes frames, because ffmpeg muxes the stream. Native NVENC is attempted on NVIDIA; otherwise encoding uses a readback fallback. Older GPUs and software Vulkan adapters are unsupported. A100, H100, H200, B200 and B300 lack the required hardware ray tracing; recency alone does not make an NVIDIA GPU suitable. Containers also need working NVIDIA Vulkan driver discovery; passing through a GPU alone may not be sufficient. If `nvidia-smi` works but Vulkan sees only llvmpipe, check the NVIDIA ICD JSON in `/etc/vulkan/icd.d` or `/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d`: its library may fail to load in a headless container. See [Vulkan driver discovery](docs/REMOTE-GPU.md#vulkan-driver-discovery). ### Mac The bundled Slang compiler requires macOS 26. Older macOS versions have not been qualified; a successful `vork --version` alone does not test Slang. In Terminal: ```sh curl -fL https://github.com/voyager-so/vork/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o /tmp/vork-install.sh sh /tmp/vork-install.sh export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" vork --version vork help ``` The same installer verifies and installs the complete Apple Silicon archive under `$HOME/.local/lib/vork`, runs setup, and adds the PATH line to your shell's startup files (`.zshenv` for zsh). Mac packages are signed with Apple Developer ID and notarised. MP4 uses VideoToolbox without ffmpeg. Install ffmpeg only for video decoding or encoding fallbacks, including MOV/ProRes fallback (`brew install ffmpeg`). ### Windows Install the NVIDIA driver for your GPU and ffmpeg (`winget install Gyan.FFmpeg`). Without winget (including Windows Server 2022), download `ffmpeg-release-essentials.zip` from [Gyan](https://www.gyan.dev/ffmpeg/builds/), extract it, and add its `bin` folder to your user PATH. Open a new PowerShell window so ffmpeg is on PATH, then: ```powershell $installer = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'vork-install.ps1' Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing https://github.com/voyager-so/vork/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 -OutFile $installer powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $installer $env:Path = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\vork;$env:Path" vork --version vork help ``` The installer itself runs in your user account without administrator rights. The installer verifies SHA256SUMS, installs under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\vork`, runs `vork setup`, and adds that folder to your user PATH so new windows find `vork`; the `$env:Path` line above covers the current one. `VORK_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` or a custom `PREFIX` leaves it alone. Windows MP4/MOV needs ffmpeg; MP4 uses its NVENC encoder when compatible, otherwise libx264. FFmpeg 9.0.2 requires NVENC API 13.1 (NVIDIA driver 610+) for hardware encoding; older drivers fall back to libx264. The cache is under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\vork`. ### Manual archive install (Windows) Download the Windows `.zip` and `SHA256SUMS` from the release page. Compare `Get-FileHash .\vork-*-windows-x64.zip -Algorithm SHA256` with its entry in `SHA256SUMS`, then unzip the entire contents into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\vork`. Add that folder to your user PATH, open a new PowerShell window, and run `vork setup`. It prints the tools/GPU report and current phase; completion is marked by `Shader setup completed`. Time depends on the GPU, driver and cache. Keep all bundled runtime companions beside the executable. ### Manual archive install (Linux or Mac) The separately downloadable `install.sh` downloads the release from GitHub; to install an archive you already have without downloading again, use the manual steps below. Download your platform's `.tar.gz` and `SHA256SUMS` from the release page into a new empty folder. In that folder, verify and install the entire archive: ```sh set -- vork-*.tar.gz test "$#" -eq 1 || exit 1 archive=$1 awk -v name="$archive" '$2 == name || $2 == "*" name' SHA256SUMS > selected.sha256 test "$(wc -l < selected.sha256 | tr -d ' ')" = 1 || exit 1 if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then sha256sum -c selected.sha256 || exit 1 else shasum -a 256 -c selected.sha256 || exit 1 fi PREFIX="$HOME/.local" mkdir tree tar -xzf "$archive" -C tree mkdir -p "$PREFIX/bin" "$PREFIX/lib/vork" cp -R tree/. "$PREFIX/lib/vork/" ln -sf "$PREFIX/lib/vork/vork" "$PREFIX/bin/vork" export PATH="$PREFIX/bin:$PATH" vork --version vork setup ``` `vork setup` prints the tools/GPU report and current phase. `Shader setup completed` marks success; time depends on the GPU, driver and cache. ### npm Requires Node.js 22.18+ and a supported GPU and driver (above). Linux and Windows video output also needs ffmpeg. ```sh npm create vork@latest my-shot cd my-shot npx vork setup npx vork render scene.json --out render.png ``` This installs the engine and TypeScript SDK into the project; no global install is needed. In an existing project, `npm install @voyager-so/vork` and use `npx vork` the same way. Keep npm's optional dependencies enabled: they carry the platform runtime. ### pip Coming soon. Use the installers above for the Python SDK in the meantime. ### First render and SDKs Start with `vork init my-shot` and enter `my-shot`, then: ```sh vork render scene.json --profile std/previs --out preview.png vork render scene.json --profile std/final --out final.png vork render scene.json --profile std/final --frame-start 0 --frame-end 23 --out clip.mp4 vork help animation vork help outputs ``` The first render of a scene with new programs can compile for several minutes. Progress reports show shader and driver pipeline preparation; allow time for it to finish. Later renders reuse compiled programs and driver caches. Compilation time depends on the scene, GPU and cache state. Frame ranges include both endpoints: `0` through `23` writes 24 frames. The simple scene is static; animation tracks make a moving clip. To try glTF import, save a model as `model.glb` beside this scene as `model.json`: ```json {"version":2,"nodes":[ {"type":"asset","file":"model.glb"}, {"type":"light","shape":"rectangle","translation":[-3,5,4],"target":[0,0,0],"energy":700,"size":4}, {"type":"camera","translation":[3,2,5],"target":[0,0,0]} ],"render":{"resolution":[640,480]}} ``` ```sh vork render model.json --profile std/final --out model.png ``` Adjust the camera and light for your model's scale. glTF files can refer to textures and buffers beside them; keep those files together. Setup warms the `vork init` starter at the default `std/final` profile on your GPU, with a ten-minute limit. Use `vork setup --skip-warmup` to check tools only. You can interrupt setup safely: completed cache entries survive and remaining pipelines compile when needed. Run setup again to continue, or use `vork setup --all` for the exhaustive catalogue without the time limit. Device cache blobs are never included in the download. Run `vork setup` again after upgrading or changing GPU drivers. It prints the tools/GPU report and current phase until `Shader setup completed`; time depends on the GPU, driver and cache. Vulkan persists its pipeline cache when supported; Metal warms the system driver cache. New scene programs can still require compilation on their first render. `VORK_CACHE_DIR` overrides the cache location. The archive includes Python and TypeScript SDK source/packages, but not their runtimes. Install the Python SDK into your authoring virtual environment, and the TypeScript SDK into your project. TypeScript requires Node 22.18+ and npm. On older Node, upgrade (recommended), or run `node --experimental-strip-types scene.ts` instead of `node scene.ts`: ```sh python3 -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install "$HOME/.local/lib/vork/python" npm install "$HOME/.local/lib/vork/sdk" ``` The SDKs install from your vork folder, not from npm or PyPI. The npm package named `vork` is unrelated, and the PyPI package only points back here. On Windows (PowerShell): ```powershell py -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\python -m pip install "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\vork\python" npm install "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\vork\sdk" ``` Use `.venv\Scripts\python scene.py` to run Python source on Windows. For a custom install, replace the default SDK paths above with your install folder. Import as `vork` in Python or `@voyager-so/vork` in TypeScript; keep the native executable on PATH. For source builds, see [`vork help build`](docs/help/build.md). ## Licence See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for the terms. Third-party notices are in [NOTICE](NOTICE). Assets and the stills in `docs/images/` retain their own licences; keep the example credits with their renders. The optional [Blender bridge](integrations/blender/) has its own GPL licence and is not part of the renderer or SDK packages.

items.title: DIYgod/pinky
items.description: Let AI agents use your phone, with you in the loop.
items.readme:
Pinky

Let any AI agent use your iPhone or Android phone, from macOS, Windows or Linux, with you in the loop.

Download · Get started · FAQ · Discord

English · 简体中文 · 日本語


A real Claude Code run on an Android 16 emulator. Pinky asks before payments by default; this run also asks before messages.

Pinky lets any agent (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor or a script) operate a real iPhone or Android phone over MCP, while you watch on your computer, approve risky steps, take over and review what happened. Approvals are enforced by Pinky's gateway, not by instructions to the agent. - **Every platform.** One app for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Windows and Linux. It drives Android phones (Android 10 to 17) and iPhones on iOS 17.4 or later: nothing to install on iOS 27 and later, and a helper installed once from Xcode on iOS 17.4 to 26, which you can also choose on iOS 27 (tried there and on Simulators, not yet on a phone below 27; [details](#phones)). - **Tiny and native.** The window is drawn by [MyGo](https://github.com/egoist/mygo) on the GPU, with no Electron and no webview: a 16–22 MB download that idles at about 70 MB of memory and 0% CPU on a Mac. - **Any agent, one click.** Settings › Agents connects Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor and more, and any agent that can use MCP servers works, on the same computer or over HTTP. - **Locked phone? Unlock it from your computer.** Save the phone's PIN in Pinky once, then confirm each unlock with Touch ID, Windows Hello or your keyring's password. Agents never see the PIN. - **Free and open source** under the Apache-2.0 license, with no account to create.

You approve the risky steps. Payments, trades and transfers wait for your click; in Settings › Safety you can have sends, orders, deletions, calls, installs, links that leave the app and settings changes wait too, or every step. Pinky spots these buttons in 10 languages. The rules run in Pinky's gateway, so an agent can't approve itself, even when text on the screen tries to talk it into it.
Off-limits by default. Banking, wallet and password-manager apps are invisible to agents, and agents can't type into password or one-time-code fields. When an agent needs a banking or wallet app for a task, it asks, and you can allow that app for that task only. Every new agent needs your approval and gets only the scope you give it.

Your phone stays yours. On Android 13 and later, agents work on a hidden second screen, so the phone's own screen stays yours, or off and locked. On older Android phones and on iPhones they use the main screen.
Take over any time. Click the mirror and the agent pauses until you hand back; on Android, touching the phone yourself pauses it too. Stop all is ⌥⌘. (Ctrl+Alt+. on Windows and Linux) from anywhere.

Every run is on the record. Each step in plain words, screenshots and a screen recording with a mark per step, exportable as an HTML report. It all stays on your computer.
iPhones too. The same gateway, approvals and records work on iOS 17.4 and later (what works). Shown here on the iOS Simulator, with deletions set to ask.
**Status:** pre-alpha. Claude Code has used real phones through it end to end (an Android phone over USB and an iPhone on iOS 27), and agents can connect over stdio or HTTP. Unlocking from the computer, background work on Android, recordings, export, Wi-Fi pairing and the phone's files are built; some of it still waits for a person to try it. See [docs/ACCEPTANCE.md](docs/ACCEPTANCE.md) for what works today and how to try it. ## Get started Install Pinky, connect your phone and add Pinky to your agent. Then ask the agent to do something on the phone, and watch it work in Pinky's window. ### What you need | | You need | | --- | --- | | **Mac** | macOS 13 or later, with Apple silicon or Intel | | **Windows** | Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit (x64) | | **Linux** | A 64-bit PC (x86-64) with Ubuntu 20.04, Debian 11 or a newer system (glibc 2.29 or later), and GTK 3 | | **Android phone** | Android 10 to 17 and a USB cable. Pinky brings its own adb; on Windows some phones need a USB driver, and on Linux USB access ([below](#usb-on-windows-and-linux)) | | **iPhone or iPad** | iOS 17.4 or later, and a USB cable to set it up; afterwards it works over Wi-Fi too ([below](#iphones-and-ipads-over-wi-fi)). Pinky prepares it itself, with Apple's developer disk image, which comes with Xcode or which Pinky can download from a third-party mirror when you ask ([below](#iphone)). On iOS 17.4 to 26 also a helper app on the iPhone ([below](#iphones-on-ios-174-to-26)) | | **Agent** | Any agent that can use MCP servers, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex or Cursor | ### 1. Download and install Pinky Get Pinky from [the latest release](https://github.com/DIYgod/pinky/releases/latest): - **Mac:** download `pinky--arm64.dmg` for a Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or later) or `pinky--amd64.dmg` for an Intel Mac. Open it and drag Pinky to Applications. With [Homebrew](https://brew.sh), `brew install --cask diygod/tap/pinky` does the same. - **Windows:** download `pinky-setup--amd64.exe` and run it. It installs Pinky for your account, without administrator rights. The installer is not signed yet, so SmartScreen may say that Windows protected your PC: choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**. To use Pinky without installing it, unzip `pinky--windows-amd64.zip` and open `Pinky.exe`. - **Linux:** on Debian and Ubuntu, download `pinky__amd64.deb` and install it with `sudo apt install ./pinky__amd64.deb`. On other systems, unpack `pinky--linux-amd64.tar.gz` into a folder of its own and run `pinky` in it. Pinky looks for new versions by itself and, on a Mac and with the Windows installer, installs them too ([Updates](#updates)). ### 2. Connect your phone Open Pinky and choose **Add phone**. A phone that is ready shows up in Pinky's window; when something is missing, the phone's page in Pinky says what. #### Android **Add phone › Android** shows these steps for your phone's brand, with its own menu names and extra switches: Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo, HONOR, HUAWEI, Samsung and Pixel, and general steps for the rest. 1. On the phone, turn on USB debugging: in Settings › About phone, tap **Build number** 7 times, then turn on **USB debugging** in Settings › System › Developer options. Some brands name these menus a little differently. 2. Plug the phone into the computer. When the phone asks whether to allow USB debugging, tap **Allow**. On Android 11 and later you can pair it over Wi-Fi instead, from **Add phone** ([when it fails](#when-pairing-over-wi-fi-fails)). Android 10 has no Wireless debugging: once it is plugged in, **Use Wi-Fi instead…** moves it to Wi-Fi ([below](#phones)). 3. Pinky offers to install Pinky Companion, its app for the phone, which makes reading the screen many times faster and lets Pinky type in any language. The phone may ask you to allow the install once. Each phone has a **Checkup**, in the ··· menu under its mirror, that lists what works and how to fix what doesn't, such as a Xiaomi's USB debugging (Security settings) switch. Taking the phone out? With Tailscale, Pinky reaches it away from home too ([how](#phones-away-from-home)).

Add phone › Android, with a Xiaomi picked.
A Redmi's Checkup, with two things to fix.
#### Android tools Pinky brings its own adb, the tool it reaches Android phones with, built from Android's source, so nothing else needs installing. When the computer has Android's platform tools already, from Android Studio, Homebrew or the system's packages, Pinky uses those, and shares their adb server with Android Studio and other tools. #### USB on Windows and Linux - **Windows:** the phone's USB debugging needs a driver. Windows installs one by itself for many phones; when it has none, Pinky lists the phone as needing setup and says which driver to install: the [Google USB Driver](https://developer.android.com/studio/run/win-usb) for Pixels, [Samsung's](https://developer.samsung.com/android-usb-driver) for Samsung phones, the [phone maker's](https://developer.android.com/studio/run/oem-usb) for others. Unplug the phone and plug it in again afterwards. - **Linux:** the computer must let Pinky open the phone's USB device, which takes udev rules for Android phones: `sudo apt install android-sdk-platform-tools-common` on Debian and Ubuntu, `android-udev` on Arch, `android-tools` on Fedora. You may also need to be in the `plugdev` group. Then plug the phone in again. Pinky says so when they are missing. #### When pairing over Wi-Fi fails When a phone works on the cable but **Pair over Wi-Fi** does not finish, the pairing page says within half a minute what Pinky sees: - **The phone hasn't shown up on the network yet:** check that Wireless debugging is on and that the phone is on the same Wi-Fi as the computer. Guest Wi-Fi, routers with AP (client) isolation and many office networks keep devices from finding each other. There, choose **Pair with a code instead**: on the phone, tap **Pair device with pairing code** and enter the IP address and port and the six-digit code it shows, which change each time that dialog opens. Pinky then needs no search to pair; if it still cannot find the phone afterwards, it asks for the IP address and port at the top of Wireless debugging (not the pairing dialog's) and connects there. If it cannot reach the phone at those addresses either, the network keeps its devices apart: use a Wi-Fi where they can reach each other, such as your home network rather than its guest network, or the cable. - **Pinky isn't allowed to look for phones on this network:** on a Mac, Pinky needs Local Network access, and macOS gives no error without it: the search just finds nothing. Choose **Open Local Network settings**, turn on Pinky under System Settings › Privacy & Security › Local Network and try again (if macOS asks whether Pinky may find devices on your local network, click **Allow**). On a Mac, a phone's **Checkup** shows this too, under **Local network**. On Windows and Linux, a firewall can block the search the same way: let Pinky use the local network, or pair with a code. - **Pinky can't look for phones on this network:** check that the computer is connected to Wi-Fi or Ethernet. - **The phone showed up, but pairing hasn't finished:** if the phone shows an error or went back to Wireless debugging, scan the code again, or pair with a code. When pairing stops with an error, the page says what adb reported: - **The phone ended the pairing before it finished** (QR code): the phone left its scanning screen, changed Wi-Fi, or something between it and the computer cut the connection; adb cannot tell which. Keep the phone on the scanning screen and try again, or choose **Pair with a code instead** next to the message. - **The phone didn't accept the pairing** (pairing code): a wrong code, or a port that is not the pairing dialog's. The address at the top of Wireless debugging is for connecting, not pairing, and adb answers the same way for both mistakes. - **Nothing at that address is waiting to pair** or **The phone stopped waiting to pair:** the pairing dialog or the scanning screen closed, or the port is wrong. Open it again and use what it shows now. - **Couldn't reach the phone at that address** or **Pinky couldn't connect to it:** the network keeps the computer and the phone apart, as above; a VPN or firewall on the computer can too. - **The adb server running on this computer is too old:** another program started an adb older than platform-tools 30. Quit it, or update it, and Pinky starts its own. Pinky writes adb's own words to its log, which **Help › Send Feedback…** attaches with the diagnostics. Pairing over Wi-Fi needs Android 11 or later; an Android 10 phone moves to Wi-Fi from the cable instead (**Use Wi-Fi instead…**, [below](#phones)). Up to Android 16, Wireless debugging turns itself off when the phone leaves the Wi-Fi network, even for another access point of it, or restarts: turn it on again, or pair again from **Add phone**. #### iPhone Pinky prepares an iPhone itself; **Add phone › iPhone** walks you through it. 1. Plug the iPhone into the computer, unlock it, tap **Trust** and enter its passcode. On Windows, install Apple Devices from the Microsoft Store (or iTunes) first; on Linux, the `usbmuxd` package. Add phone says when they are missing. 2. On the iPhone, turn on **Developer Mode** in Settings › Privacy & Security: Pinky makes the switch appear there. The iPhone restarts; unlock it, tap **Turn On** and enter the passcode. 3. Pinky mounts Apple's developer disk image on the iPhone and lists it as ready. An iPhone on iOS 27 keeps the image when it restarts; below iOS 27 Pinky mounts it again after each restart, once you unlock the iPhone. The developer disk image comes with [Xcode](https://apps.apple.com/app/xcode/id497799835), Apple's free app for developers, and Pinky does not ship it. On a Mac, install Xcode once and open it: Pinky uses the image it installs, and Xcode never has to run again. An iPhone on iOS 27 or later needs the image of Xcode 27 or later: Apple's signing server no longer signs older ones, and Add phone then says which image Pinky used and how to get a newer one. On Windows and Linux, copy `/Library/Developer/DeveloperDiskImages/iOS_DDI` from such a Mac into Pinky's folder ([where](docs/notes/ios.md#preparing-a-phone-without-xcode)). Without either, or when Apple refuses the image Pinky found (Xcode's, or one copied into Pinky's folder), Add phone offers to download the image from a third-party mirror, github.com/doronz88/DeveloperDiskImage (Xcode 27.0 beta 4, 32 MB, kept by the author of pymobiledevice3, not by Apple), only when you click Download; Pinky checks every file against the checksum it expects, and from then on uses it instead of an image Apple refused. On iOS 27 and later, no app gets installed on the iPhone. Checked on the iPhone 13 mini (iOS 27.0.1): Pinky mounting Xcode's image itself (in about 1.5 s, after the image had been taken off), keeping the image already on the phone, and that the iPhone keeps the image when it restarts. Not yet tried on a phone: the downloaded image, the Developer Mode switch, iPhones below iOS 27, and pairing an iPhone on Windows. Contributors have used an iPhone and an iPad on iOS 27.2 on Linux (Arch Linux), and an iPhone on iOS 27.2 on Windows 11, on the cable and over Wi-Fi, with the image already on them. #### iPhones and iPads over Wi-Fi Pinky also uses an iPhone or iPad over Wi-Fi while it is on the same Wi-Fi as the computer, and the computer lists it there, which it does once Wi-Fi connections are on for the phone. Pinky turns them on when you plug the phone in and it trusts the computer: it is the same setting as Finder's **Show this iPhone when on Wi-Fi**, so a phone already set up that way stays as it is. It is on by default; **Settings › Phones › Use iPhones and iPads over Wi-Fi** turns it off, which leaves the phones' setting alone. If a phone doesn't show up on Wi-Fi when you unplug it, its **Checkup** says where it stands under **Wi-Fi**: whether its Wi-Fi connection is on and whether Pinky turned it on, why Pinky couldn't, and whether this computer sees the phone on Wi-Fi. - An iPhone or iPad Pinky has used keeps working when you unplug it, as the same phone with its settings: Pinky moves it to Wi-Fi by itself, and back to the cable when you plug it in, and an agent's task goes on; its calls wait a few seconds meanwhile. - One Pinky has not used, such as a family member's iPad paired with this computer, shows as **Found on Wi-Fi**. Pinky reads its name, model and iOS version and does nothing else, and agents don't see it, until you choose **Use**, which sets it up over Wi-Fi, or **Ignore**, which keeps it off the list until you plug it in. - A locked iPhone or iPad on Wi-Fi shows as **Locked on Wi-Fi**, and Pinky connects to it once you unlock it: while it sleeps it drops off the network every minute or so, and connecting to it then lights its screen. - Setting one up over Wi-Fi: trusting the computer needs the cable, and so does making the Developer Mode switch appear while it is hidden (on a phone used with Xcode it shows already). Turning Developer Mode on happens on the phone, and Pinky mounts the developer disk image over Wi-Fi too, in about 9 s instead of 1.5 s. **Add phone › iPhone** says which step needs the cable. Over Wi-Fi each step is slower than on the cable, screenshots most of all. Measured on an iPad Pro 11-inch (3rd generation, iPadOS 27.0.1), Wi-Fi against the cable: a swipe shows on screen after 80 to 210 ms (60 to 90 ms), the home screen reads in 0.6 to 2.6 s (0.5 to 0.6 s), a screenshot takes 5 s (1 s), and 0.2 % of the video's packets were lost (none). Unplugging moved a running task to Wi-Fi in about 5 s, and plugging in moved it back in 2 to 6 s ([details](docs/notes/ios.md#wi-fi)). On a Mac, the system's device service, usbmuxd, can lose an iPhone on Wi-Fi after its connection broke once (its Wi-Fi turned off and on, say), and not look for it again for up to about an hour; Finder loses it too. Pinky notices when a phone you use is on the network but no longer listed, shows it as **Lost on Wi-Fi**, and offers **Restart device service…** on its page: after you confirm, macOS asks for an administrator's password, and every iPhone and iPad, also on a cable, disconnects for a second or two. `sudo killall usbmuxd` in Terminal does the same. Right after you unplug a phone it says so within about 10 seconds; it waits a minute otherwise, as a phone that wakes comes back by itself. A phone you unplug that this computer doesn't see on Wi-Fi at all shows as **Not seen on Wi-Fi**, with what may hide it: it's asleep, on another network or one that keeps devices apart (guest networks, some routers), a VPN, or Pinky not allowed on the local network. On Linux and Windows, the system's device service does not list iPhones and iPads on Wi-Fi by itself: on Linux (the `usbmuxd` package) it lists them only on the cable, and on Windows (Apple Devices or iTunes) only while they are on the cable too. So there Pinky runs a small device service of its own in front of the system's, while it uses phones over Wi-Fi: it finds the phones paired with this computer on the network and connects to them directly, and passes everything about phones on a cable to the system's. All of Pinky's connections to iPhones and iPads go through it then, on the cable too. There is nothing to install or set up for it beyond the system's own (`usbmuxd` on Linux, Apple Devices on Windows). If you run a device service that lists phones on Wi-Fi itself, such as netmuxd, and start Pinky with `USBMUXD_SOCKET_ADDRESS` pointing at it (`unix:///path/to/socket` or `tcp://127.0.0.1:port`), Pinky uses that one instead and runs none of its own. While Pinky opens a phone, or moves it between the cable and Wi-Fi, it shows **Connecting** or **Moving to Wi-Fi** rather than offline. Over Wi-Fi Pinky reads text from the live picture rather than from screenshots, which take about 5 s there. An iPhone or iPad without a passcode never reads as locked, so after it has dropped off the network to sleep, Pinky connects to it only once it has been back for 30 seconds. #### iPhones on iOS 17.4 to 26 Below iOS 27, an iPhone takes taps and typing from a computer only through a helper app on the phone: WebDriverAgent, which you build and install once from Xcode with your Apple ID ([how](docs/notes/ios.md#installing-the-webdriveragent-helper)). With a free Apple ID it has to be installed again every 7 days: two days before, the phone's page and its checkup remind you, and once it has run out the phone shows as needing setup and says why ([how to install it again](docs/notes/ios.md#when-the-helpers-signature-runs-out)). It has not been tried on an iPhone below iOS 27 yet. Without it, Pinky can only show and read the screen (on a Mac) and open apps: no taps, swipes or typing. iOS 17.3 and earlier are not supported. ### 3. Add Pinky to your agent In Pinky, open **Settings › Agents** and click **Connect** next to your agent. Pinky finds Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Copilot CLI, Windsurf (Devin Desktop) and Gemini CLI on your computer and adds itself to the agent's MCP servers, by the app's own path: with the agent's own command where it has one, such as `claude mcp add`, or in its settings file, which Pinky copies first and changes only in Pinky's entry. It also installs Pinky's agent guide, [SKILL.md](docs/SKILL.md), where the agent reads skills. Until an agent is connected, a card in Pinky's sidebar offers to do it, or says where to get one.

- **Claude Desktop:** Connect opens Pinky's extension in Claude Desktop; click **Install** there. Double-clicking `pinky-.mcpb` from the [release page](https://github.com/DIYgod/pinky/releases/latest) does the same. - **Other agents:** **Settings › Agents › Add an agent by hand** shows the command for your copy of Pinky, with buttons that copy it. Add an MCP server (stdio) that runs it. In a JSON config, with the Homebrew cask or a Linux package: ```json { "mcpServers": { "pinky": { "command": "pinkyctl", "args": ["mcp"] } } } ``` Claude Code in a terminal: `claude mcp add --scope user pinky -- pinkyctl mcp`. Most agents read the guide from `~/.agents/skills/pinky/SKILL.md`, Claude Code from `~/.claude/skills/pinky/SKILL.md`. The command is `pinkyctl`, not `pinky`: many computers already have another program named `pinky`. An agent on another computer or in a container can connect over HTTP instead ([how](docs/mcp.md#over-http)). [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md#connecting-an-agent) says what Connect changes for each agent. ### 4. Try it Ask the agent to do something on your phone, for example "Open Messages on my phone and tell Sam I'm running late." The first time an agent connects, Pinky asks whether to allow it and what it may do. Payments wait for your click in Pinky's window; in Settings › Safety you can have sends, deletions and more wait too. No phone at hand? Quit Pinky and start it with two scripted demo phones (a payment to approve, a blocked banking app, a password field): `/Applications/Pinky.app/Contents/MacOS/Pinky --fake` on a Mac, `pinkyctl --fake` on Linux, or `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\Pinky\Pinky.exe" --fake` in PowerShell on Windows. ## Using Pinky ### Phones - **Android:** connected over USB or Wi-Fi ([above](#android)). Pinky works over adb and a bundled scrcpy server. Its companion app, which ships with Pinky, reads the screen in about 70 ms instead of 2 s and types any language without the clipboard: the phone's page offers to install it (the phone may ask you to allow it once). Its accessibility service is on only while an agent works on the phone, as banking apps refuse to run next to one ([why](#faq)). On Android 13 and later, agents work on a background display, so the phone's own screen can stay off and locked. Text that an app draws without describing it to the accessibility tree, as in mini-programs and other web pages inside super-apps, games and maps, is read from the screen's pixels (OCR) on macOS and Windows, so agents can read it and tap it. Pinky reads a blocked app this way only once you allow it for the task, never a locked phone, and keeps no picture. - **Wi-Fi on Android 10:** Android 10 has no Wireless debugging. Plug the phone in and choose **Use Wi-Fi instead…** in the ⋯ menu under its picture (or in Settings › Phones): Pinky has the phone's adb listen on the network (`adb tcpip`, port 5555), connects to it at its Wi-Fi address and says when you can unplug it. It connects again by itself when the phone is back on the network, also at a new address. While it is on, any computer on the same network can try to connect to the phone: if the phone asks **Allow USB debugging?** when you are not connecting it yourself, tap **Cancel**, and use it only on Wi-Fi you trust. It lasts until the phone restarts; then plug it in once and choose **Use Wi-Fi again**. **Stop the Wi-Fi connection** in the same menu turns it off ([details](docs/away-from-home.md#wi-fi-without-wireless-debugging)). - **iPhone:** connected over USB or Wi-Fi ([above](#iphones-and-ipads-over-wi-fi)) and prepared by Pinky ([above](#iphone)); iPads work the same way. What Pinky can do depends on the iOS version and on how Pinky connects, which you can choose for each iPhone in Settings › Phones (Automatic picks by version, as below): | iOS | How | What works | Tested on | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 27 and later | Xcode's Device Hub protocol; nothing installed on the phone | Everything. Typing pastes the text and puts your clipboard back | iPhone 13 mini, iOS 27.0.1 | | 17.4 and later, with the helper | The WebDriverAgent helper, installed once from Xcode ([how](docs/notes/ios.md#installing-the-webdriveragent-helper)): automatic on iOS 17.4 to 26, your choice on 27 | Everything, and the phone shares no screen, so banking apps that refuse screen sharing keep working (DBS digibank and China Merchants Bank in testing). Slower than Device Hub: a home screen reads in about 7 s instead of under 0.5 s, a tap takes 0.5 to 0.8 s. Now and then iOS asks for the passcode on the phone before the helper starts. The live picture needs macOS | iPhone 13 mini, iOS 27.0.1, with the helper chosen; iOS 18.5 and 26.5 Simulators. Not yet on a phone below iOS 27 | | 17.4 to 26, without it | The developer services alone; nothing installed | Watching (a few frames a second, macOS only), reading the screen (placed by OCR, macOS only) and opening apps. No tapping, swiping, typing or Home: the phone offers no input without the helper | The same services on iOS 27.0.1; not yet on a phone below iOS 27 | | 17.3 and earlier | | Not supported: before 17.4 the connection needs administrator rights, and iOS 16 and earlier need a developer disk image that current Xcode no longer includes | | The helper is Appium's WebDriverAgent, signed with your own Apple ID. The signature lasts 7 days with a free Apple ID and a year with a paid developer account. Pinky reads on the iPhone when it runs out: two days before, the phone's page and its checkup remind you to install the helper again from Xcode, and once it has run out the phone shows as needing setup and says why, instead of failing to start the helper ([how](docs/notes/ios.md#when-the-helpers-signature-runs-out)). - **Screen sharing on iPhone:** while Pinky streams an iPhone's screen, iOS tells apps that the screen is being shared, and some banking apps (DBS digibank and China Merchants Bank among them) refuse to run or warn you. Pinky streams it while the phone's page or tile is open in Pinky, while an agent works on it, and for 30 seconds after; then such apps work again. Over CoreDevice, agents cannot use them. Connect that iPhone through the WebDriverAgent helper instead (Settings › Phones): the phone then shares no screen, and agents can use those apps too. - **Locked phones:** Pinky never keeps a phone awake. It wakes the screen before a step; save the phone's PIN in Settings › Phones to unlock it from the computer with Touch ID. Agents never see the PIN. On Android this is checked on AOSP-style lock screens (LineageOS on a Mi 10 Pro, the Android 10, 16 and 17 emulators); the lock screens of Xiaomi, Samsung, OPPO, OnePlus, vivo, Honor and Huawei are only covered by tests made from what is known of them, and where Pinky cannot read the PIN pad with confidence it enters nothing ([details](docs/notes/integration.md#unlocking-other-android-phones)). - **Files:** on Android, agents copy files between the phone's Pinky folder (`/sdcard/Pinky`, the only place on the phone they may reach) and a folder on the computer, and copying to the phone asks you first. Pictures copied there show in the phone's gallery and photo pickers, so an agent can attach them in a chat app. An agent on another computer cannot reach that folder, so it sends Pinky the file first: small files in the call, larger ones to a one-time link Pinky gives it. Copying the file to the phone then asks you as usual ([details](docs/mcp.md#uploading-a-file)). Not on iPhones. - **Removing a phone:** **Remove this phone…** in the phone's ⋯ menu (also on its page while it is offline, on its tile in All phones, in its right-click menu in the sidebar and in Settings › Phones) takes it off the list and deletes its saved PIN and its settings. Its tasks, screenshots and recordings stay in Activity unless you tick the box to delete them too, and a task running on it stops. A phone on a cable comes back at once, as a new phone, until you unplug it. A phone on Wi-Fi is disconnected and stays off the list, even when adb connects it again by itself; to add it back, pair it again in Add phone or plug it in. An iPhone or iPad on Wi-Fi stays off the list until you plug it in. Pinky does not unpair the phone from your computer: its USB or wireless debugging pairing, or the iPhone's trust, stays for other apps ([details](docs/notes/gateway.md#removing-a-phone)). ### Phones away from home An Android phone does not have to be on the computer's network. With [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) on the computer and on the phone, signed in to the same account, Pinky reaches the phone through it: leave the computer at home and take the phone out, on mobile data or another Wi-Fi. Android runs one VPN at a time, so keep other VPN and proxy apps off on the phone: they turn Tailscale off. 1. Set the phone up once while it is near the computer, by cable or on the same Wi-Fi: **Settings › Phones › Use away from home › Turn on…**. **Add phone › Android › Phone not on this network? Use Tailscale** walks you through Tailscale on both sides and lists the phones on your tailnet. 2. Pinky has the phone's adb listen on the network (`adb tcpip`, port 5555) and connects to the phone at its Tailscale address. It uses that connection whenever the phone has no connection on the computer's network, so the phone stays in the list as you leave. 3. The phone's adb then takes connections on every network the phone joins, from the computers it already trusts; any other computer makes the phone ask. Only the way through Tailscale is encrypted. It lasts until the phone restarts, and **Turn off** stops it at once. Pinky only reads Tailscale's status and never changes its settings. 4. **Keep this computer awake for phones away** (Settings › Phones, on by default) stops the computer's idle sleep while a phone is connected through Tailscale. A MacBook still sleeps when its lid closes. At home, Tailscale is as fast as Wi-Fi; away, the phone's upload carries the picture, so Pinky streams lighter through Tailscale (1 Mbit/s), and on a weak 4G hotspot each step takes seconds. Details, measurements, data use and what to do when it does not connect: [docs/away-from-home.md](docs/away-from-home.md). An agent can be away from the computer too: [Remote agents](docs/mcp.md#over-http). ### Updates Pinky looks for a new version at launch and every few hours, and shows a card with what changed, **Update now** and **Later**. With Settings › Advanced › **Update automatically** (on by default) it installs it by itself once no agent is working and nobody has used Pinky for ten minutes, and it updates Pinky Companion on Android phones that are free; its accessibility service stays off until the next task. A Pinky Companion signed with the public key that its builds had until 8 November 2026 is uninstalled and installed again, signed with Pinky's private key, and Pinky tells you; on a phone that asks before installing apps over USB, the phone's page says why and waits for your **Update**. After an update, **What's new** lists the changes since the version you had (from [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md), or its Chinese version, [CHANGELOG.zh-CN.md](CHANGELOG.zh-CN.md), when Pinky is in Chinese). - **macOS:** Pinky.app replaces itself after checking the download's checksum, that it is signed by Pinky's developer and that Apple notarized it, and goes back to the old version if the new one does not start. The Homebrew cask's copy updates itself the same way, and `brew upgrade` leaves it alone while it is current. A copy run from the disk image or from a folder you cannot write to says how to update it instead. - **Windows:** a Pinky that its installer installed runs the new installer quietly, after checking its checksum, starts the new version and goes back to the old one if that does not start. The portable copy downloads the installer for you. - **Linux:** Pinky downloads the release for you to install. - **Terminal:** `pinkyctl update` installs an update while Pinky is not running; `pinkyctl daemon` only logs that one is out. Details: [docs/notes/updates.md](docs/notes/updates.md). ### Usage statistics, crash reports and feedback Pinky shares anonymous usage statistics (counters such as tasks run, tools called and phones connected, about once a day, with a random install id) and crash reports; turn both off in Settings › Privacy or with `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`. Screens, typed text, app names, phone names and ids, PINs and file names are never sent. Help › Send Feedback… opens a GitHub issue with your message and diagnostics filled in, which you read and submit yourself. [docs/TELEMETRY.md](docs/TELEMETRY.md) lists everything. ## FAQ
Which agents work with Pinky? Any agent that can use MCP servers: over stdio, by running `pinkyctl mcp`, or over HTTP with an agent token ([how](docs/mcp.md#over-http)). **Settings › Agents** connects Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor and other agents it finds on your computer in one click. Claude Code is the one that has used real phones end to end so far. Pinky brings no model of its own: your agent does the thinking.
Can an agent approve its own risky step, or be talked into it? No. The rules run in Pinky's gateway, between the agent and the phone. A step that needs you comes back to the agent as `approval_pending`, and nothing happens on the phone until you click **Allow** in Pinky; the agent has nothing it could send to confirm it. Before acting, Pinky checks that the button is still where it was, and no answer within 60 seconds means no. Pinky finds these buttons by their labels in 10 languages, so an unusual one could slip through: for more control, Settings › Safety has **Ask before every action** and **Read-only mode**.
What can't agents see? Banking, wallet and password-manager apps, from a list that comes with Pinky and that you can add to in Settings › Safety, where you pick the app from those on your phones: agents get no screen from them, and their notifications are hidden, in the notification shade and on the lock screen too. Where another screen shows a blocked app, as its notification in the shade or in a banner, or its card in recent apps, the agent reads only that something is hidden there, and the screenshots it gets, and those in Activity, cover it with a gray box (screen recordings, which stay on your computer, show it as it was). Agents can't type into password or one-time-code fields. When an agent needs a banking or wallet app for a task, Pinky asks you first. If you allow it, the agent may open and read that app for the rest of the task, what your rules ask about there still asks, and Pinky keeps no screenshots or recordings of it: to read text that only its pixels show, Pinky looks at its screen in memory and gives the agent the text, never the picture. Password managers are never offered. One-time codes are masked before an agent reads them: in a text message, an email, a notification or anywhere else on the screen, "Your code is 482913" reaches the agent as "Your code is ••••••", and the screenshots it gets, and those in Activity, have the code covered with a gray box. Prices, phone numbers, dates and numbers in text that is not about a code stay as they are. Screen recordings, which stay on your computer and never go to agents, show codes as they were. You can turn this off in Settings › Safety › Hide codes from agents.
Does my phone's screen go to the cloud? Not through Pinky. Screenshots, recordings and history stay on your computer, for 30 days unless you change it in Settings › Privacy, where you can also delete them. What the agent reads goes to the agent you chose, as with any tool you give it. Pinky's anonymous usage statistics never include screens, typed text or app names ([above](#usage-statistics-crash-reports-and-feedback)).
What does Pinky install on my phone? On Android, Pinky Companion, when you click Install; Pinky keeps it up to date and turns its accessibility service on only while an agent works ([why](#faq)). On an iPhone, no app on iOS 27 and later: Pinky mounts Apple's developer disk image, as Xcode does. On iOS 17.4 to 26, the WebDriverAgent helper, which you install once from Xcode ([how](docs/notes/ios.md#installing-the-webdriveragent-helper)).
